figures.name: Production Possibilities Curve — Constant Opportunity Cost (Fig 3.1)
figures.what_shows: Tom's max combinations of fish and coconuts; a straight-line PPC for two goods.
figures.axes: x-axis = quantity of fish; y-axis = quantity of coconuts.
figures.shifts: Straight line slope = −3/4 means constant opportunity cost (3/4 coconut per fish). Points ON the curve = productively efficient; INSIDE = feasible but inefficient (e.g., unemployment); OUTSIDE = infeasible.
figures.memorize: Slope of a linear PPC equals the opportunity cost of the good on the x-axis in terms of the good on the y-axis (sign aside).

figures.name: Increasing Opportunity Cost PPC (Fig 3.2)
figures.what_shows: Bowed-out (concave) PPC where each additional fish costs more coconuts than the last.
figures.axes: x = fish, y = coconuts.
figures.shifts: Bowed outward shape arises from specialization of resources (some inputs are better suited to one good than the other).
figures.memorize: Real-world PPCs are bowed out because inputs are heterogeneous; "perfectly suited inputs get used up first."

figures.name: Economic Growth — Outward Shift of PPC (Fig 3.3)
figures.what_shows: Original PPC and a new PPC shifted outward, enabling more of BOTH goods.
figures.axes: x = fish, y = coconuts.
figures.shifts: Outward shift caused by (1) more resources, or (2) better technology. A technology-specific improvement may shift only one intercept, not both.
figures.memorize: Economic growth = outward shift of PPC. A movement from inside to a point on the same PPC is NOT economic growth — it's recovery / falling unemployment.

figures.name: Production Possibilities for Two Castaways (Fig 4.1)
figures.what_shows: Tom (slope −3/4) vs. Hank (slope −2). Tom has absolute advantage in BOTH goods; Hank has comparative advantage in coconuts.
figures.axes: x = fish, y = coconuts (each panel).
figures.shifts: Different slopes = different opportunity costs = gains from trade possible.
figures.memorize: Comparative advantage, NOT absolute advantage, drives gains from trade. The flatter PPC has comparative advantage in the x-axis good.

figures.name: Comparative Advantage and International Trade (Fig 4.3)
figures.what_shows: US (flatter PPC) has comparative advantage in pork; Canada (steeper) in aircraft. After trade, both countries consume OUTSIDE their original PPCs.
figures.axes: x = pork (millions of tons); y = aircraft.
figures.shifts: Specialization + trade allows consumption beyond own PPC (though production stays on PPC).
figures.memorize: Trade lets a country CONSUME outside its PPC, even though it cannot PRODUCE outside it.

figures.name: U.S. Unemployment Rate, 1989–2013 (Fig 2.1)
figures.what_shows: Time series; shaded recession bars overlay an unemployment rate that swings between ~4% and ~10%.
figures.axes: x = year; y = unemployment rate (%).
figures.shifts: Unemployment spikes during recessions, declines (with lag) in expansions.
figures.memorize: Unemployment is a LAGGING indicator that moves COUNTER-cyclically to output.

figures.name: Real GDP per Capita, 1900–2013 (Fig 2.2)
figures.what_shows: Long-run growth path of US real GDP per capita; >8x growth over the period.
figures.axes: x = year; y = real GDP per capita in 2005 dollars.
figures.shifts: Persistent upward slope dwarfs business-cycle wiggles; the Great Depression is the only visible recession at this scale.
figures.memorize: Long-run growth > short-run fluctuations. Standard of living tracks per-capita REAL (inflation-adjusted) GDP.

figures.name: Demand Schedule and Demand Curve (Fig 5.1)
figures.what_shows: Downward-sloping demand curve for cotton from a hypothetical demand schedule.
figures.axes: x = quantity (billions of pounds); y = price ($/lb). Note: price on VERTICAL axis even though it's typically the independent variable — economist convention.
figures.shifts: Downward slope = law of demand.
figures.memorize: PRICE IS ON THE Y-AXIS in economics demand/supply graphs (violates the math convention).

figures.name: Movement Along vs. Shift of the Demand Curve (Fig 5.3)
figures.what_shows: A → B is a movement along D1 (price change); A → C is a shift to D2 (non-price factor change).
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = price.
figures.shifts: A change in PRICE → movement along; a change in any OTHER demand determinant → shift.
figures.memorize: "Demand" = the whole curve; "quantity demanded" = a single point. Confusing these is the #1 introductory mistake.

figures.name: Individual vs. Market Demand Curve (Fig 5.5)
figures.what_shows: Market demand = horizontal sum of individual demand curves.
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = price.
figures.shifts: At each price, add the quantities (not the prices) across consumers.
figures.memorize: Sum HORIZONTALLY — at a given price, add up Q_i across all consumers.

figures.name: Supply Curve for Cotton
figures.what_shows: Quantity of cotton supplied at each price; canonical upward-sloping supply.
figures.axes: x = quantity supplied (billions of lbs); y = price (per lb).
figures.shifts: Positive slope (law of supply). A price change is a movement along; non-price determinants (I-RENT) shift the whole curve.
figures.memorize: A rightward shift = "increase in supply" (more supplied at every price), NOT a shift "down."

figures.name: Increase in Supply (S1 → S2)
figures.what_shows: Technology improvement shifts S right.
figures.axes: Same as Fig 6.1.
figures.shifts: S2 lies to the right of S1; at every price, Qs is larger.
figures.memorize: "Increase in supply" means rightward, not downward — a common AP trap.

figures.name: Movement Along vs. Shift
figures.what_shows: A→B is a movement along S1 (price change); A→C is a shift to S2 (non-price change).
figures.axes: Price (y) vs. quantity (x).
figures.shifts: Distinguishes ΔQs (movement) from ΔSupply (shift).
figures.memorize: A price change NEVER shifts the curve whose own price is on the axis.

figures.name: Market Equilibrium
figures.what_shows: S∩D at point E gives equilibrium price P* and quantity Q*.
figures.axes: Price (y), quantity (x).
figures.shifts: Above P*, surplus pushes price down; below P*, shortage pushes price up.
figures.memorize: Equilibrium = market-clearing = Qd = Qs; both buyers and sellers are individually optimizing.

figures.name: Simultaneous Shifts
figures.what_shows: D and S shifting in opposite directions — one of price/quantity is determinate, the other ambiguous.
figures.axes: Price (y), quantity (x).
figures.shifts: Magnitude of the larger shift determines the ambiguous variable.
figures.memorize: Opposite-direction shifts → price determinate, Q ambiguous. Same-direction shifts → Q determinate, price ambiguous.

figures.name: Price Ceiling on Apartments
figures.what_shows: Binding ceiling below P* causes shortage (Qd>Qs).
figures.axes: Monthly rent (y), apartments (x).
figures.shifts: Horizontal line at the ceiling price; shortage = Qd − Qs at ceiling.
figures.memorize: Only ceilings BELOW equilibrium bind; they cut Q traded AND create shortage.

figures.name: Price Floor on Butter
figures.what_shows: Binding floor above P* causes surplus (Qs > Qd).
figures.axes: Price per pound (y), millions of lbs (x).
figures.shifts: Horizontal line at floor; surplus is the horizontal gap at the floor price.
figures.memorize: Floors ABOVE equilibrium bind. Both ceilings AND floors reduce Q traded.

figures.name: Quota on Taxi Rides — the "Wedge"
figures.what_shows: Vertical quota line creates a wedge between demand price ($6) and supply price ($4). Wedge = quota rent.
figures.axes: Fare (y), rides per year (x).
figures.shifts: Quota rent = vertical distance between D and S at the quota Q. Deadweight loss = triangle between curves to the right of the quota.
figures.memorize: Quota rent = Pd(Q_quota) − Ps(Q_quota). Equal to the market price of a tradable license.

figures.name: Expanded Circular-Flow Diagram
figures.what_shows: Money flows among households, firms, government, rest of world via factor, product, and financial markets.
figures.axes: N/A (flow diagram).
figures.shifts: Inflows must equal outflows at every node ("what goes in must come out").
figures.memorize: Disposable income = Income + Transfers − Taxes; Private savings + Foreign lending → Investment + Govt borrowing.

figures.name: Two Methods of Calculating U.S. GDP
figures.what_shows: Value-added breakdown vs. expenditure breakdown; both sum to GDP.
figures.axes: $ billions (y), method (x).
figures.shifts: Net exports were −$494B (2013), shown extending below axis.

figures.name: Unemployment Rate, 1948–2013
figures.what_shows: U.S. unemployment fluctuates; rises in every recession.
figures.axes: Year (x), unemployment rate % (y).
figures.shifts: Shaded bars = recessions; rate always rises during them.
figures.memorize: Unemployment rate NEVER reaches zero, even at boom peaks — frictional unemployment is permanent.

figures.name: Effect of Minimum Wage on Labor Market
figures.what_shows: Binding wage floor W_F > W_E creates structural unemployment (Qs > Qd).
figures.axes: Wage (y), quantity of labor (x).
figures.shifts: Q_S − Q_D = structural unemployment caused by the floor.
figures.memorize: Minimum wage REDUCES employment (Q_D < Q_E) AND creates surplus labor — fewer people work than would without the floor.

figures.name: Price Level vs. Inflation Rate
figures.what_shows: Price level keeps rising even when inflation rate falls (as long as inflation is positive).
figures.axes: Year (x), price level (left y), inflation rate (right y).
figures.shifts: Falling inflation ≠ falling prices; disinflation just slows the climb.
figures.memorize: Price level matters less than the RATE OF CHANGE; that's the core macro insight.

figures.name: CPI, PPI, and GDP Deflator
figures.what_shows: Three inflation measures move together; PPI is most volatile.
figures.axes: Year (x), % change (y).
figures.shifts: PPI swings most because commodity/energy prices dominate it.
figures.memorize: PPI is the "early warning signal" for inflation because producers reprice fastest.

figures.name: Consumption Function (Figure 16.2, p. 200)
figures.what_shows: A household's planned consumer spending as a linear function of current disposable income.
figures.axes: x-axis = household current disposable income; y-axis = household consumer spending.
figures.shifts: Upward-sloping line; vertical intercept = autonomous consumer spending (what you'd spend with zero income, financed by borrowing/savings); slope = MPC. Shifts up with expected higher future income or rising aggregate wealth; shifts down with the opposite.
figures.memorize: Slope of the consumption function = MPC; intercept = autonomous consumption.

figures.name: Aggregate Demand Curve (Figure 17.1, p. 209)
figures.what_shows: Negative relationship between aggregate price level and real GDP demanded by all four sectors.
figures.axes: x-axis = Real GDP; y-axis = Aggregate price level (GDP deflator).
figures.shifts: Downward-sloping due to (1) wealth effect and (2) interest rate effect — NOT the substitution/income effects of microeconomics. Shifts from changes in expectations, wealth, stock of physical capital, fiscal policy, monetary policy.
figures.memorize: AD slopes down because of wealth + interest-rate effects ONLY. Substitution between goods is irrelevant here because all prices change together.

figures.name: Short-Run Aggregate Supply (Figure 18.1, p. 218)
figures.what_shows: Positive relationship between aggregate price level and real GDP supplied while nominal wages are sticky.
figures.axes: x-axis = Real GDP; y-axis = Aggregate price level.
figures.shifts: Upward-sloping because fixed nominal wages make profit per unit rise when prices rise. Shifts (PEAR mnemonic): Productivity, Expectations of inflation, Actions (taxes/subsidies), Resource prices (wages, commodities).
figures.memorize: SRAS upward slope = sticky wages + fixed short-run costs. A commodity-price increase shifts SRAS left (negative supply shock).

figures.name: Long-Run Aggregate Supply (Figure 18.3, p. 222)
figures.what_shows: Vertical line at potential output Y_P; in the long run, all prices (including wages) are flexible so price level has no effect on output.
figures.axes: x-axis = Real GDP; y-axis = Aggregate price level.
figures.shifts: Perfectly vertical at Y_P. Shifts right with more/better resources or technological progress (long-run growth).
figures.memorize: LRAS is vertical at potential output. The economy's actual output fluctuates around Y_P, not on it.

figures.name: AD–AS Short-Run Equilibrium (Figure 19.1, p. 229)
figures.what_shows: Intersection of AD and SRAS gives short-run equilibrium (P_E, Y_E).
figures.axes: x-axis = Real GDP; y-axis = Aggregate price level.
figures.shifts: Demand shocks move P and Y in the SAME direction; supply shocks move them in OPPOSITE directions (the key diagnostic).
figures.memorize: Same-direction co-movement of P and Y ⇒ demand shock. Opposite-direction ⇒ supply shock (stagflation when negative).

figures.name: Long-Run Self-Correction from a Demand Shock (Figure 19.5, p. 233)
figures.what_shows: A negative AD shock creates a recessionary gap; in the long run, falling nominal wages shift SRAS right until output returns to Y_P at a lower price level.
figures.axes: x-axis = Real GDP; y-axis = Aggregate price level.
figures.shifts: Three points: E1 (initial LR equilibrium) → E2 (short-run after demand shock, recessionary gap) → E3 (new LR equilibrium at Y_P with lower P).
figures.memorize: The economy is self-correcting — output gap → 0 in the long run via nominal wage adjustment.

figures.name: Expansionary Fiscal Policy Closes a Recessionary Gap (Figure 20.4, p. 242)
figures.what_shows: Government uses ↑G, ↓T, or ↑transfers to shift AD right back to Y_P.
figures.axes: x-axis = Real GDP; y-axis = Aggregate price level.
figures.shifts: AD1 → AD2 right; new equilibrium at Y_P with higher P. Mirror image (Figure 20.5) for contractionary fiscal policy closing an inflationary gap.
figures.memorize: Fiscal policy shifts AD, not SRAS. For supply shocks, there is no easy fiscal fix — it's a policy trilemma.

figures.name: Money Creation T-Account (Figure 25.3, p. 284)
figures.what_shows: When $1,000 cash deposit becomes a checkable deposit, bank holds 10% as reserves and lends out 90%, increasing money supply by the loan amount.
figures.axes: T-account (Assets left = Loans + Reserves; Liabilities right = Deposits).
figures.shifts: Initial deposit: money supply unchanged (currency down $1,000, deposits up $1,000). After loan: money supply up $900 because $900 in new cash is now in circulation AND the $1,000 deposit still exists.
figures.memorize: Banks create money through the loan step, not the deposit step.

figures.name: The Monetary Base and the Money Supply
figures.what_shows: Two overlapping concepts—monetary base (bank reserves + currency in circulation) vs. money supply (checkable deposits + currency in circulation), sharing only currency in circulation.
figures.axes: Venn-style diagram (no axes); two circles.
figures.shifts: Bank reserves are in the base but NOT in M1; checkable deposits are in M1 but NOT in the base. Currency in circulation is the only overlap.
figures.memorize: Bank reserves ≠ money supply; checkable deposits ≠ monetary base; money supply > monetary base because each reserve dollar backs multiple deposit dollars.

figures.name: The Federal Reserve System
figures.what_shows: Map of 12 Federal Reserve districts plus Board of Governors in D.C.
figures.axes: Geographic map.
figures.shifts: New York Fed conducts open-market operations; Alaska and Hawaii belong to San Francisco district.
figures.memorize: Fed = Board of Governors (7 members, 14-yr terms) + 12 regional banks; FOMC = Board + 5 regional presidents (NY always; 4 of other 11 rotate).

figures.name: 27.1 / 27.2: Fed T-account & Open-Market Operations (pp. 299–300)
figures.what_shows: Fed assets = Treasury bills; liabilities = monetary base. Open-market purchase increases banks' reserves and the base; sale decreases them.
figures.axes: T-accounts (assets vs. liabilities).
figures.shifts: Fed BUYS Treasuries → reserves & base ↑ → MS ↑ via multiplier. Fed SELLS → reserves & base ↓ → MS ↓.
figures.memorize: The Fed never buys Treasuries directly from the government—only from commercial banks—to avoid "monetizing" deficits.

figures.name: 28.1 / 28.2 / 28.3: Money Demand & Equilibrium (pp. 306–309)
figures.what_shows: Downward-sloping MD curve in (Q of money, nominal r) space; vertical MS curve set by Fed; equilibrium at intersection.
figures.axes: x = quantity of money; y = NOMINAL interest rate r.
figures.shifts: MD shifts right with ↑ price level, ↑ real GDP, more cash-friendly institutions; shifts left with ATMs/credit cards. MS shifts via Fed action.
figures.memorize: Vertical axis is the NOMINAL interest rate (because the opportunity cost of holding money includes inflation erosion).

figures.name: Equilibrium in the Loanable Funds Market
figures.what_shows: Upward-sloping supply (savers) and downward-sloping demand (borrowers) intersect at equilibrium r and Q of loanable funds.
figures.axes: x = quantity of loanable funds; y = interest rate (real or nominal, given fixed expected inflation).
figures.shifts: D shifts right with ↑ rate of return on projects, ↑ government deficits. S shifts right with ↑ private saving, ↑ capital inflows.
figures.memorize: Projects with rate of return ≥ equilibrium r get funded; lenders willing to lend at ≤ equilibrium r are matched. Government deficit shifts D right → crowding out.

figures.name: The Fisher Effect
figures.what_shows: A rise in expected inflation shifts both S and D for loanable funds UP by the same amount, raising the nominal interest rate one-for-one while leaving real r and equilibrium Q unchanged.
figures.axes: Quantity of loanable funds (x), nominal interest rate (y).
figures.shifts: S and D both shift up by Δπᵉ percentage points.
figures.memorize: Δ nominal r = Δ expected inflation; real r unchanged; equilibrium quantity Q* unchanged.

figures.name: Actual vs. Cyclically Adjusted Budget Deficit
figures.what_shows: Cyclically adjusted deficit (what it would be at potential output) fluctuates less than the actual deficit because recessions amplify deficits via automatic stabilizers.
figures.axes: Year (x), deficit as % of GDP (y).
figures.shifts: Actual deficit spikes during recessions; cyclically adjusted line is smoother.
figures.memorize: Cyclically adjusted balance strips out business-cycle effects—a better gauge of long-run fiscal sustainability.

figures.name: Expansionary vs. Contractionary Monetary Policy
figures.what_shows: A flowchart: ↑ MS → ↓ r → ↑ I → ↑ Y (via multiplier) → AD shifts right; reverse for contractionary.
figures.axes: AD-AS diagram (price level vs. real GDP).
figures.shifts: Expansionary monetary policy shifts AD right; contractionary shifts AD left.
figures.memorize: AD curve shifts in the SAME direction as the money supply curve.

figures.name: Short-Run and Long-Run Effects of an Increase in Money Supply
figures.what_shows: ↑ MS shifts AD right → short-run Y > potential, P↑. Eventually nominal wages rise, SRAS shifts left, Y returns to potential at a higher P.
figures.axes: Aggregate price level (y) vs. Real GDP (x).
figures.shifts: AD₁→AD₂; SRAS₁→SRAS₂; final equilibrium on LRAS at higher P only.
figures.memorize: Long-run effect = price level rises proportionally; real GDP unchanged (monetary neutrality).

figures.name: The Classical Model of the Price Level
figures.what_shows: In high-inflation economies, prices adjust so quickly that we ignore the short-run SRAS movement—economy jumps directly from E₁ to E₃.
figures.axes: Aggregate price level (y) vs. Real GDP (x).
figures.shifts: SRAS treated as effectively vertical under high inflation.
figures.memorize: Classical model is a good approximation under HIGH inflation, poor under low inflation.

figures.name: 34.2 / 34.5 / 34.6: Short-Run and Long-Run Phillips Curves (pp. 365–370)
figures.what_shows: SRPC is downward-sloping (unemployment vs. inflation trade-off). Expected inflation shifts SRPC up by an equal amount. LRPC is vertical at the NAIRU.
figures.axes: x = unemployment rate; y = inflation rate.
figures.shifts: ↑ expected inflation shifts SRPC up 1-for-1; negative supply shocks shift SRPC up.
figures.memorize: No long-run trade-off—any attempt to push unemployment below NAIRU produces ever-accelerating inflation.

figures.name: Japan's Lost Decade & Zero Bound
figures.what_shows: Japan's inflation and interest rate trend toward zero from late 1990s onward.
figures.axes: Year (x); interest rate / inflation rate (y).
figures.shifts: Both lines drift downward and bunch near zero.
figures.memorize: When nominal r hits 0 and the economy is still depressed, monetary policy is in a "liquidity trap."

figures.name: Fiscal Policy with a Fixed Money Supply
figures.what_shows: Crowding out: expansionary fiscal policy is partly neutralized when M is fixed because money demand rises, driving up r and reducing investment.
figures.axes: Panel (a) Real GDP (x) vs. Aggregate Price Level (y); Panel (b) Quantity of money (x) vs. Interest rate (y).
figures.shifts: AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2 (smaller than multiplier predicts); MD shifts right from MD1 to MD2 along vertical MS; r rises from r1 to r2.
figures.memorize: With a fixed money supply, fiscal expansion is partially crowded out — multiplier shrinks.

figures.name: The Velocity of Money
figures.what_shows: Velocity (nominal GDP/M1) was smooth before 1980, then became erratic — undermining monetarism.
figures.axes: Year (x) vs. Velocity of M1 (y).
figures.shifts: Roughly linear trend pre-1980, volatile post-1980.
figures.memorize: Unstable V after 1980 killed the monetarist case for a fixed M-growth rule.

figures.name: Economic Growth in U.S., India, and China
figures.what_shows: Real GDP per capita (2005 dollars, log scale), 1910–2010, for the three countries.
figures.axes: Year (x) vs. Real GDP per capita (log scale, y).
figures.shifts: U.S. on a long upward trend; China surges after 1980; India rises but stays below 1910 U.S. level.
figures.memorize: Log scale = equal % changes look equal; China only recently reached the U.S.'s 1910 standard of living.

figures.name: Physical Capital and Productivity
figures.what_shows: Aggregate production function (productivity curve) exhibits diminishing returns to physical capital.
figures.axes: Physical capital per worker (x) vs. Real GDP per worker (y).
figures.shifts: Upward-sloping concave curve (positive slope, decreasing).
figures.memorize: Each successive $30K of K/worker yields a smaller boost in Y/worker (e.g., +$20K then +$10K).

figures.name: Technological Progress and Productivity Growth
figures.what_shows: Technological progress shifts the productivity curve upward (from "1940 tech" to "2010 tech").
figures.axes: Physical capital per worker (constant $, x) vs. Real GDP per worker (constant $, y).
figures.shifts: Upward shift of the entire production function = rising total factor productivity (TFP).
figures.memorize: Movement along curve = more K/worker; shift of curve = TFP / technology.

figures.name: Economic Growth on a PPC
figures.what_shows: Outward shift of PPC = long-run economic growth.
figures.axes: Quantity of fish (x) vs. Quantity of coconuts (y).
figures.shifts: Bowed-out original PPC shifts outward to "New PPC."
figures.memorize: Growth = outward PPC shift; inside the PPC = unemployed resources / recession.

figures.name: Long-Run Growth and the LRAS Curve
figures.what_shows: Long-run economic growth as repeated rightward shifts of the LRAS.
figures.axes: Real GDP (x) vs. Aggregate price level (y).
figures.shifts: Series of vertical LRAS curves at YP1, YP2, YP3 with each subsequent curve farther right.
figures.memorize: LRAS is vertical at potential output; growth shifts it right.

figures.name: The Balance of Payments Circular Flow
figures.what_shows: Money flows between U.S. and rest-of-world: current account (goods/services/income/transfers) and financial account (assets).
figures.axes: No axes — circular flow diagram with green (current) and red (financial) arrows.
figures.shifts: Inflows must equal outflows in total.
figures.memorize: Current account + Financial account = 0.

figures.name: International Capital Flows in Loanable Funds
figures.what_shows: When capital is mobile, interest rates equalize across two countries; capital flows from low-r (Britain) to high-r (U.S.).
figures.axes: Quantity of loanable funds (x) vs. Interest rate (y), drawn side-by-side for each country.
figures.shifts: Equilibrium r converges (e.g., to 4%) from initial 2% (UK) and 6% (US); horizontal gap in each market = capital inflow or outflow.
figures.memorize: Capital flows narrow international interest-rate gaps.

figures.name: The Foreign Exchange Market
figures.what_shows: Equilibrium exchange rate set by demand for and supply of a currency.
figures.axes: Quantity of U.S. dollars (x) vs. Exchange rate (€/US$, y).
figures.shifts: Downward-sloping demand for dollars; upward-sloping supply of dollars; equilibrium at point E.
figures.memorize: Higher €/US$ = dollar appreciation = U.S. exports fall, imports rise.

figures.name: Real vs. Nominal Exchange Rates, Mexico
figures.what_shows: Nominal peso/dollar rate rose massively 1990–2013, but real rate barely changed because Mexican inflation outpaced U.S. inflation.
figures.axes: Year (x) vs. Pesos per US$ (y).
figures.shifts: Nominal line rises sharply; real line is roughly flat.
figures.memorize: Trade flows respond to the *real* exchange rate, not nominal.

figures.name: A Ceramic Plates Quota
figures.what_shows: Effect of a 2-million-plate import quota on the U.S. ceramic plates market.
figures.axes: x = Quantity of plates (millions); y = Price ($).
figures.shifts: Pink "US + Quota" supply = domestic supply shifted right horizontally by 2 million above $9 (the world price). Equilibrium with quota: P = $12, Q = 6M (4M domestic + 2M imports).
figures.memorize: A quota produces the *same* price/quantity outcome as an equivalent tariff but generates **no government revenue** — the wedge becomes private rent for quota holders.

figures.name: Analysis Starting Points
figures.what_shows: Three valid AD-AS starting points — long-run equilibrium, recessionary gap, inflationary gap.
figures.axes: x = Real GDP; y = Aggregate price level.
figures.shifts: AD downward, SRAS upward, LRAS vertical at Yp. Recessionary gap: SR equilibrium left of LRAS; inflationary gap: right of LRAS.
figures.memorize: Always identify the starting point first; LRAS is vertical at potential output regardless of price level.

figures.name: Monetary and Fiscal Policy Close Output Gaps
figures.what_shows: AD shifts right to close recessionary gap; AD shifts left to close inflationary gap.
figures.axes: Real GDP vs. aggregate price level.
figures.shifts: Expansionary policy → AD1→AD2 right (P up, Y up). Contractionary → AD1→AD2 left (P down, Y down).
figures.memorize: Fiscal & monetary policy work *initially* through AD only; SRAS shifts later via nominal-wage adjustment if no policy intervenes.

figures.name: The Demand for Vaccinations
figures.what_shows: A small movement from A($20, 10M) to B($21, 9.9M) illustrating PED computation.
figures.axes: x = Quantity of vaccinations; y = Price.
figures.shifts: Downward-sloping D; |%ΔQ|/|%ΔP| = 1%/5% = 0.2 → highly inelastic.
figures.memorize: PED is reported as an absolute value (drop the negative).

figures.name: Two Extreme Cases of PED
figures.what_shows: Perfectly inelastic D (vertical line at Q=1B shoelaces) vs. perfectly elastic D (horizontal line at $5 for pink tennis balls).
figures.axes: Standard P-Q.
figures.shifts: Vertical → PED = 0; Horizontal → PED = ∞.
figures.memorize: "I"-shaped (vertical) = Inelastic; "E"-shaped (horizontal middle stroke) = Elastic.

figures.name: Elasticity Changes Along a Linear Demand Curve
figures.what_shows: Upper section of linear D is elastic, lower is inelastic, midpoint is unit-elastic; TR maximized at midpoint.
figures.axes: Top panel P-Q; bottom panel total-revenue bars.
figures.shifts: TR rises along inelastic section, peaks at unit-elastic midpoint, falls along elastic section.
figures.memorize: Along a *linear* downward-sloping D curve, elasticity is NOT constant — it varies from ∞ at the P-intercept to 0 at the Q-intercept.

figures.name: 49.3 / 49.4 / 49.5: Consumer Surplus (pp. 525–527)
figures.what_shows: CS = triangular area below D, above P; rectangle-plus-triangle gain from a price fall.
figures.axes: P-Q.
figures.shifts: Price fall → CS rises by rectangle (original buyers' savings) + triangle (new buyers' gain).
figures.memorize: CS = ½ × base × height for a linear demand curve.

figures.name: 50.6 / 50.7: Excise Tax Incidence (pp. 504–505 in chunk)
figures.what_shows: Tax on producer shifts S up by tax; tax on consumer shifts D down by tax — outcome identical.
figures.axes: P-Q hotel rooms.
figures.shifts: Wedge of size T between Pc (price consumers pay) and Pp (price producers receive). Q falls from Qe to Qt.
figures.memorize: Statutory incidence ≠ economic incidence; legal payer is irrelevant.

figures.name: 50.11 / 50.12: Tax Surplus Loss and DWL (pp. 510–511)
figures.what_shows: Excise tax shrinks CS (by rectangle A + triangle B) and PS (by rectangle C + triangle F); government gets A+C; DWL = B+F.
figures.axes: P-Q.
figures.shifts: DWL triangle points toward the efficient (pre-tax) quantity.
figures.memorize: DWL = ½ × T × (Qe − Qt); zero if either D or S is perfectly inelastic.

figures.name: Total and Marginal Utility
figures.what_shows: TU rises, peaks (Cassie at 8 clams = 64 utils), then falls; MU declines monotonically and turns negative at the 9th clam.
figures.axes: x = Quantity of clams; y = Utils.
figures.shifts: MU curve slopes downward (diminishing MU); TU peaks where MU = 0.
figures.memorize: TU is maximized at the quantity where MU = 0 (free-good case); otherwise constrained by budget.

figures.name: Marginal Utility per Dollar / Optimal Consumption
figures.what_shows: Sammy's MUc/Pc and MUp/Pp curves cross at C (2 clams, 6 potatoes) where both equal 2 utils/$.
figures.axes: Dual horizontal axis (clams L→R, potatoes R→L); y = MU/$ (utils).
figures.shifts: Both curves downward-sloping; optimum is the intersection.
figures.memorize: Optimal bundle: MUx/Px = MUy/Py simultaneously satisfying the budget.

figures.name: The Firm's Profit-Maximizing Quantity of Output
figures.what_shows: For a price-taker, profit is maximized at the output where MC crosses the horizontal MR = P line.
figures.axes: x = quantity (bushels), y = price/cost per bushel.
figures.shifts: MC has "swoosh" shape (falls then rises); MR is horizontal at market price.
figures.memorize: Optimal point E is where MC = MR = P; produce the largest Q where MR ≥ MC if no exact crossing.

figures.name: Production Function & Total Product Curve
figures.what_shows: TP rises with labor at a decreasing rate (diminishing returns).
figures.axes: x = quantity of labor (workers), y = quantity of output (bushels of wheat).
figures.shifts: Slope of TP = MPL; flattens as MPL declines. Increasing the fixed input shifts TP up.
figures.memorize: Slope of TP curve at any point = marginal product of labor (MPL).

figures.name: MPL Curve
figures.what_shows: MPL declines as more workers are added.
figures.axes: x = workers, y = MPL (bushels per worker).
figures.shifts: Downward-sloping when diminishing returns are present; shifts up if fixed input increases.
figures.memorize: Diminishing returns ≠ negative returns; MPL may still be positive, just smaller.

figures.name: 55.3 & 55.4: U-shaped ATC and the Cost-Curve Family (pp. 593–594)
figures.what_shows: MC crosses ATC and AVC at their respective minimums from below.
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = cost per unit.
figures.shifts: ATC is U-shaped (spreading effect vs. diminishing returns effect); AFC continuously falls.
figures.memorize: MC = ATC at minimum ATC (analogous to grade-point average rule).

figures.name: "Swoosh" MC with U-shaped AVC and ATC
figures.what_shows: Realistic MC first falls (specialization) then rises (diminishing returns).
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = cost.
figures.shifts: MC dip → AVC U-shape; MC still passes through min ATC and min AVC.
figures.memorize: "Swoosh" shape comes from initial increasing returns due to specialization.

figures.name: Short-Run vs. Long-Run ATC
figures.what_shows: LRATC is the lower envelope of an infinite family of SRATC curves.
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = cost per unit.
figures.shifts: Downward slope → economies of scale; upward slope → diseconomies of scale.
figures.memorize: Each SRATC touches LRATC at one point — the output level for which that fixed cost is optimal.

figures.name: Short-Run Individual Supply Curve
figures.what_shows: A perfectly competitive firm's supply curve = MC above min AVC; below that, supply drops to zero.
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = price/cost.
figures.shifts: Break-even price = min ATC; shut-down price = min AVC.
figures.memorize: Below min AVC the firm shuts down; between min AVC and min ATC it operates at a loss to cover some FC.

figures.name: 60.3 / 60.4 / 60.5: Long-Run Industry Supply (pp. 643–646)
figures.what_shows: LRS is horizontal (constant cost), upward-sloping (increasing cost), or downward-sloping (decreasing cost).
figures.axes: x = industry quantity, y = price.
figures.shifts: Entry shifts SR supply right; LRS is always flatter (more elastic) than SR supply.
figures.memorize: In long-run PC equilibrium, each firm produces at min ATC and earns zero economic profit.

figures.name: Monopoly Profit Maximization
figures.what_shows: Monopolist sets Q where MR = MC, then charges the price on the demand curve at that Q.
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = price/cost/MR.
figures.shifts: MR lies below D because of the price effect on prior units.
figures.memorize: P > MR = MC for a monopolist (vs. P = MR = MC for a price-taker).

figures.name: Welfare Loss Under Monopoly
figures.what_shows: Monopoly transfers part of CS to producer surplus and creates a deadweight-loss triangle.
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = price.
figures.shifts: DWL is the yellow triangle between QM and QC, bounded by D and MC.
figures.memorize: DWL exists because units where willingness-to-pay > MC go unproduced.

figures.name: Regulating a Natural Monopoly
figures.what_shows: Price ceiling at P*R (where D crosses ATC) eliminates monopoly profit and maximizes CS without bankrupting the firm.
figures.axes: x = quantity, y = price.
figures.shifts: ATC slopes downward over relevant range; setting P = MC would force losses.
figures.memorize: Best regulated price for natural monopoly = where D intersects ATC (zero profit, max CS).

figures.name: Two Types of Airline Customers
figures.what_shows: With perfect price discrimination, a monopolist charges each consumer group its willingness to pay, capturing all surplus.
figures.axes: x = quantity of tickets (2,000 business + 2,000 students = 4,000); y = price/cost ($).
figures.shifts: Step-shaped demand curve at $550 and $150; MC=ATC horizontal at $125. Two rectangles B (business) and S (students) represent profit.
figures.memorize: A perfectly price-discriminating monopolist produces the efficient (allocatively optimal) quantity — no deadweight loss.

figures.name: Price Discrimination Panels
figures.what_shows: As the number of distinct prices charged rises (2 → 3 → many), profit rectangles fill the entire area under demand above MC.
figures.axes: x = quantity; y = price/cost.
figures.shifts: Panel (c) shows profit = triangle between D and MC (entire consumer surplus captured).
figures.memorize: More prices charged → more consumer surplus extracted → lowest price approaches MC.

figures.name: Demand Schedule for Lysine
figures.what_shows: A monopolist (cartel) maximizes revenue at Q=60M lbs, P=$6, TR=$360M (assumed MC=0).
figures.axes: Price ($) vs. Quantity (millions of lbs).
figures.shifts: TR is hump-shaped, peaks at midpoint of linear demand.
figures.memorize: With MC=0, total-revenue maximization = profit maximization, occurring where MR=0 (midpoint of linear demand).

figures.name: 65.1/65.2: Payoff Matrix (Prisoners' Dilemma) (pp. 685–686)
figures.what_shows: Two firms (or prisoners) each have a dominant strategy to cheat/confess; the Nash equilibrium leaves both worse off than mutual cooperation.
figures.axes: Rows = Player 1's actions; Columns = Player 2's actions. Each cell = (Player 1 payoff, Player 2 payoff).
figures.shifts: "Circle trick" — circle best response per column for row player and per row for column player. Two circles in one cell = Nash equilibrium.
figures.memorize: A Nash equilibrium is NOT necessarily Pareto-efficient. Confess/Cheat is the dominant strategy even though Don't/Cooperate maximizes joint payoff.

figures.name: 65.3/65.5/65.6: Avoidance, Differing Choices, Differing Payoffs (pp. 688–691)
figures.what_shows: Games can have (a) no dominant strategy and two Nash equilibria, (b) one player with a dominant strategy and one Nash equilibrium, (c) weakly dominant strategies.
figures.memorize: Two circles in a row → dominant strategy for row player; two circles in a column → dominant strategy for column player.

figures.name: Tit-for-Tat Repeated Game
figures.what_shows: In a repeated game, "tit-for-tat" supports tacit collusion: cooperate first, then mimic opponent.
figures.memorize: Always-cheat dominates in a one-shot game; tit-for-tat dominates over a long horizon. Long-run cooperation > short-run cheating.

figures.name: Monopolistic Competition Short-Run
figures.what_shows: Panel (a) profitable firm (D > ATC at Q*); Panel (b) loss-minimizing firm (D < ATC everywhere).
figures.axes: x = quantity; y = price/cost/MR. Profit/loss rectangle between P and ATC at Q*.
figures.shifts: Downward-sloping D and MR (below D); U-shaped ATC; upward MC. Profit-max at MR=MC.
figures.memorize: Always set Q where MR=MC, then read P off the demand curve (not the MR curve!).

figures.name: Long-Run Zero-Profit Equilibrium
figures.what_shows: D is tangent to ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity QMC; P = ATC, so π = 0.
figures.shifts: Tangency point Z lies on the downward-sloping (left) portion of ATC → excess capacity.
figures.memorize: In LR monop. comp., D is TANGENT to ATC, NOT crossing it. P > MC (allocatively inefficient) AND Q < minimum-ATC Q (productively inefficient/excess capacity).

figures.name: Perfect vs. Monopolistic Competition Long Run
figures.what_shows: PC firm produces at min ATC with P=MC; MC firm produces left of min ATC with P>MC.
figures.memorize: Both earn zero economic profit in LR, but only PC achieves productive AND allocative efficiency.

figures.name: Factor Distribution of Income in the U.S. 2013
figures.what_shows: 69.2% compensation of employees, 10.5% proprietors, 9.6% interest, 6.0% corporate profit, 4.6% rent.
figures.memorize: Labor's share has been ~70% for 40+ years — remarkably stable.

figures.name: Marginal Revenue Product Curve
figures.what_shows: MRPL slopes down due to diminishing marginal returns; firm hires where MRPL = W.
figures.axes: x = quantity of labor; y = wage rate / MRPL.
figures.memorize: A firm's MRP curve IS its individual factor demand curve.

figures.name: Land and Capital Markets
figures.what_shows: Land supply is steep (inelastic); capital supply is flatter (elastic). Equilibrium rental rate at S=D.
figures.memorize: Land's inelastic supply → land tax has NO deadweight loss; entire burden falls on landowners.

figures.name: Economic Rent with Fixed Supply
figures.what_shows: Vertical supply at 512 acres; rental rate is determined entirely by demand. Entire payment = economic rent.
figures.memorize: Economic rent = payment above the minimum needed to employ the factor. Producer surplus is its goods-market analog.

figures.name: Backward-Bending Labor Supply
figures.what_shows: Panel (a) substitution effect dominates (upward-sloping); Panel (b) income effect dominates (downward-sloping).
figures.memorize: Leisure is a normal good. At high wages, the income effect can dominate, causing the labor supply curve to bend backward.

figures.name: 71.4/71.5: Monopsony (pp. 747–748)
figures.what_shows: MFCL lies ABOVE the (upward-sloping) labor supply curve. Firm hires where MRPL = MFCL, then sets W on the supply curve (not on MFC).
figures.memorize: Monopsony wage < competitive wage AND monopsony employment < competitive employment. Wage is BELOW MRPL (worker exploitation).

figures.name: Earnings by Education, Gender, Ethnicity
figures.what_shows: Education raises earnings within every demographic group; for each level, White males earn most, women less than men of same group.
figures.memorize: Even after controlling for education, gaps persist — explained by experience, compensating differentials, discrimination, and market power.

figures.name: Median Earnings by Gender and Ethnicity, 2013
figures.what_shows: Bar chart of 2013 annual median earnings: White male $48,620, Hispanic $31,408, African-American $34,424, Female (all ethnicities) $38,480.
figures.axes: y = annual median earnings (USD); x = demographic group.
figures.shifts: Levels differ persistently; women earn ~79% of men, African-Americans ~71%, Hispanics ~65% of White male earnings.
figures.memorize: Persistent wage gaps exist even after accounting for some marginal-productivity factors → motivates compensating differentials, human capital, efficiency wages, discrimination.

figures.name: Socially Optimal Quantity of Pollution
figures.what_shows: Upward-sloping MSC of pollution and downward-sloping MSB of pollution intersect at Q_OPT where MSC = MSB = $200.
figures.axes: y = marginal social cost / benefit ($/ton); x = tons of pollution emissions.
figures.shifts: MSC slopes up (nature handles low pollution but harm rises with quantity); MSB slopes down (additional avoidance gets progressively more expensive, so each extra ton emitted is worth less).
figures.memorize: Optimal pollution is NOT zero; it occurs where MSC = MSB.

figures.name: Why a Market Economy Produces Too Much Pollution
figures.what_shows: Without intervention polluters push emissions to Q_MKT where MSB = 0 but MSC = $400, leaving large net social loss.
figures.axes: Same as 74.1.
figures.shifts: Polluters internalize only private benefit (=MSB to them) and treat their MC of polluting as $0, so they pollute until MSB hits zero.
figures.memorize: Q_MKT > Q_OPT; the deadweight loss = triangle between MSC and MSB from Q_OPT to Q_MKT.

figures.name: In Pursuit of the Efficient Quantity of Pollution
figures.what_shows: A Pigouvian tax of $200/ton (= MSC at Q_OPT) shifts polluters from Q_MKT down to Q_OPT.
figures.axes: y = MSC/MSB ($); x = tons of pollution.
figures.shifts: Tax raises polluter's MC from 0 to $200; equivalently, cap-and-trade issuing Q_OPT permits yields a permit price of $200.
figures.memorize: Optimal Pigouvian tax = marginal external cost at Q_OPT = MSC at Q_OPT.

figures.name: Environmental Standards vs. Emissions Taxes
figures.what_shows: Two plants A and B with different MB curves (MB_A < MB_B). Panel (a): uniform standard forces each to cut 50% → MB_A=$150, MB_B=$300 (inefficient). Panel (b): $200 tax → A cuts to 200 tons, B cuts to 400 tons (efficient).
figures.axes: y = MB to individual polluter ($/ton); x = tons of emissions.
figures.shifts: Efficient outcome requires MB equalized across polluters; only price-based instruments achieve this.
figures.memorize: Tax/permit systems beat standards because they equate marginal benefit of pollution across all polluters.

figures.name: Positive Externalities and Consumption — flu shots
figures.what_shows: MSB = D shifted up by marginal external benefit (MEB). Market produces Q_MKT < Q_OPT → DWL triangle. A Pigouvian subsidy = MEB raises producer price to P_OPT and lowers consumer price to P_CNS.
figures.axes: y = price, marginal social benefit ($); x = quantity of flu shots.
figures.shifts: MSB curve sits above demand by the vertical distance MEB.
figures.memorize: MSB = MPB + MEB; under-consumption in unregulated market.

figures.name: Negative Externalities and Production — livestock
figures.what_shows: MSC = S shifted up by MEC. Q_MKT > Q_OPT. A Pigouvian tax = MEC raises consumer price to P_OPT and lowers producer price to P_PRD.
figures.axes: y = price, marginal social cost ($); x = quantity of livestock.
figures.shifts: MSC above S; demand = MPB = MSB (no external benefit).
figures.memorize: MSC = MPC + MEC; production externalities → MSC > S, over-production.

figures.name: Four Types of Goods Matrix
figures.what_shows: 2×2 matrix of excludable/non- × rival/nonrival → private goods, public goods, common resources, artificially scarce goods.
figures.axes: Columns = rivalry; rows = excludability.
figures.shifts: Wheat = private; sewage/national defense = public; clean water/biodiversity = common; pay-per-view/software = artificially scarce.
figures.memorize: Only private goods are efficiently supplied by free markets.

figures.name: A Public Good (street cleanings)
figures.what_shows: Marginal SOCIAL benefit curve is the **VERTICAL** sum of individual MPB curves (Ted + Alice). Efficient quantity where MSB = MSC = $6 → 5 cleanings/month.
figures.axes: y = MB/MC ($); x = quantity of street cleanings.
figures.shifts: Vertical (not horizontal) summation because nonrival in consumption — both consume the same unit.
figures.memorize: Public good demand aggregates VERTICALLY; private good demand aggregates HORIZONTALLY.

figures.name: A Common Resource (fish)
figures.what_shows: MSC lies ABOVE the supply curve (S = MPC); market produces Q_MKT > Q_OPT (overuse).
figures.axes: y = price of fish; x = quantity of fish.
figures.shifts: Parallel to negative production externality: each user's MSC > MPC by the depletion cost imposed on others.
figures.memorize: Common resources are OVERUSED in markets; fixes = tax, tradable licenses, assign property rights.

figures.name: Price Setting for a Regulated (Natural) Monopoly
figures.what_shows: Downward-sloping ATC and MC (MC below ATC). MC pricing → P = MC at Q1 yields loss (P < ATC). Average-cost pricing → P = ATC at Q2 yields zero economic profit, but Q2 < Q1 (below allocatively efficient quantity).
figures.axes: y = price, cost per unit; x = quantity.
figures.shifts: Economies of scale → ATC falling → MC < ATC.
figures.memorize: Marginal-cost pricing is allocatively efficient but requires subsidy; average-cost pricing breaks even but undersupplies.

figures.name: U.S. Poverty Rate 1959–2012
figures.what_shows: Sharp fall in the 1960s–early 1970s, then no clear trend; 2012 rate higher than 1973.
figures.memorize: Poverty threshold adjusts for cost of living but NOT for standard of living, so rising prosperity does not automatically pull people out.

figures.name: The Lorenz Curve
figures.what_shows: Cumulative % income vs. cumulative % population; 45° line = perfect equality. Gini = A / (A+B), where A = area between line of equality and Lorenz curve.
figures.shifts: Greater inequality → curve bows further below 45° line → larger A → higher Gini.
figures.memorize: Gini = 0 (perfect equality), Gini = 1 (one person has all income). U.S. Gini in 2012 ≈ 0.477.

figures.name: Income Inequality Around the World
figures.what_shows: World map of Gini coefficients — highest in Latin America/Africa, lowest in Scandinavia (~0.25), U.S. unusually high among rich nations.
figures.memorize: Sweden ~0.25, U.S. ~0.477, Brazil ~0.6.

figures.name: D.1 — Ingrid's 3-D Utility "Hill"
figures.what_shows: Total utility as a 3-D surface over consumption of two goods (rooms, restaurant meals), with contour lines connecting equal-utility bundles.
figures.axes: horizontal axes = quantity of rooms and quantity of restaurant meals; height = total utility (utils).
figures.shifts: Contour lines at fixed utility levels (150, 300, 450, 600, 750, 900, 1,050 utils). Points A (3 rooms, 30 meals) and B (6 rooms, 15 meals) both sit on the 450-util contour.
figures.memorize: Bundles on the same contour = the consumer is indifferent between them; "higher hill" = more utility.

figures.name: D.2 / D.3 — Indifference Curve & Indifference Curve Map
figures.what_shows: 2-D projection of the contour lines — each curve I_n is the set of bundles giving the same total utility.
figures.axes: x = rooms, y = restaurant meals.
figures.shifts: Curves are downward-sloping and convex (bowed toward origin). Curves farther from origin = higher utility. Two indifference curves never cross.
figures.memorize: Four properties of ordinary-good indifference curves: (1) never cross, (2) higher is better, (3) downward-sloping, (4) convex (diminishing MRS).

figures.name: D.5 — Changing Slope of an Indifference Curve
figures.what_shows: Same indifference curve traced from V (2 rooms, 30 meals) to Z (6 rooms, 10 meals). Trade goes from "10 meals for 1 room" (V→W) down to "2 meals for 1 room" (Y→Z).
figures.axes: x = rooms, y = meals.
figures.shifts: Slope flattens as you move right — this IS diminishing MRS, which is a direct consequence of diminishing marginal utility.
figures.memorize: |slope of indifference curve| = MRS = MU_x / MU_y.

figures.name: D.6 / D.7 — Optimal Consumption: Tangency of Budget Line & Indifference Curve
figures.what_shows: Budget line BL (income $2,400, rooms $150, meals $30) tangent to highest reachable indifference curve I_2 at optimal bundle A (8 rooms, 40 meals).
figures.axes: x = rooms, y = meals.
figures.shifts: Income change → parallel shift of BL (slope unchanged). Relative price change → BL rotates (slope changes). At optimum: slope of BL = slope of IC.
figures.memorize: Relative price rule: MU_R/MU_M = P_R/P_M (equivalently MU_R/P_R = MU_M/P_M, the optimal consumption rule).

figures.name: FLH-1 — "Saving to Be a Millionaire" Case Study
figures.what_shows: Steve (starts at 25, $400/mo, 7%) vs. Jessica (starts at 35, $850/mo, 7%) — both hit $1M at age 65.
figures.axes: x = age band; y = account balance ($).
figures.shifts: Steve contributes $192,000 total; Jessica contributes $306,000 total (60% more) for the same outcome.
figures.memorize: A 10-year head start beats a 113% increase in monthly contribution — compounding is the moat.

figures.name: FLH-2 — Sarah vs. Tom Retirement Saving
figures.what_shows: Sarah ($200/mo from age 25) ends with ~$693,201; Tom ($300/mo from age 35) ends with ~$447,107 — both at 8%.
figures.axes: x = age; y = portfolio value ($).
figures.memorize: Starting 10 years earlier with LESS monthly contribution still produces $250,000 more — time > amount.

concepts.name: Scarcity
concepts.definition: A resource is scarce when there isn't enough of it to satisfy all the ways society wants to use it. Scarcity = unlimited wants meeting limited resources.
concepts.why: It's the prime mover of all economics — no scarcity, no need to choose, no economics.
concepts.mnemonic: "SCARCE = Society Can't Always Receive Complete Enjoyment." If everyone got everything, economists would be unemployed.
concepts.related: Opportunity cost, choice, resources, trade-off.

concepts.name: The Four Factors of Production (Resources)
concepts.definition: Land (natural resources), Labor (human effort), Capital (manufactured goods used to make other goods — NOT money), Entrepreneurship (risk-taking, innovation, organization).
concepts.why: Every PPC, every aggregate production function, every growth model invokes these four. AP graders love to trick students by calling "money" capital — wrong.
concepts.mnemonic: "LLCE = Lazy Llamas Catch Earthworms." Or: imagine a farm — the Land you stand on, the Labor of farmhands, the tractors (Capital), and the farmer-Entrepreneur deciding what to plant.
concepts.related: Capital (don't confuse with financial capital), production function.

concepts.name: Opportunity Cost
concepts.definition: The value of the next-best alternative forgone when you make a choice. ALL costs are opportunity costs.
concepts.why: It is the "real" cost of any decision and underlies the PPC, comparative advantage, and marginal analysis.
concepts.mnemonic: "Opportunity Cost = Opportunity LOST." Picture LeBron James walking past a college library — his opportunity cost of attending college was a $13M NBA contract.
concepts.related: Marginal analysis, comparative advantage, sunk cost (NOT an opportunity cost).

concepts.name: Marginal Analysis
concepts.definition: Comparing the marginal benefit (MB) and marginal cost (MC) of doing a little bit MORE of something. Rule: do it if MB ≥ MC; stop where MB = MC.
concepts.why: It is the engine of every optimization problem in economics — utility max, profit max, hiring labor, public policy.
concepts.mnemonic: "ADDITIONAL = MARGINAL." Whenever the AP says "one more," translate it instantly to "marginal."
concepts.related: Marginal cost, marginal benefit, marginal utility, MRP.

concepts.name: Positive vs. Normative Economics
concepts.definition: Positive = descriptive ("what IS"); has a right/wrong answer. Normative = prescriptive ("what SHOULD be"); involves value judgments.
concepts.why: Most policy disagreements are normative; this distinction tells you whether evidence can settle a question.
concepts.mnemonic: "Normative = Norms" (values, ought, should). "Positive = Photograph" (objective snapshot of reality).
concepts.related: Models, value judgments, economic forecasting.

concepts.name: Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics
concepts.definition: Micro = decisions of individual agents (households, firms) and individual markets. Macro = economy-wide aggregates (GDP, unemployment, inflation, growth).
concepts.why: Determines which model toolkit to apply on a question.
concepts.mnemonic: "MICRO = MY decisions; MACRO = MASS decisions." Or think Micro-scope vs. Macro-cosm.
concepts.related: Economic aggregates, GDP, business cycle.

concepts.name: Business Cycle
concepts.definition: Alternation of recessions (downturns: falling output & employment) and expansions/recoveries (upturns). A depression is an unusually deep, prolonged downturn.
concepts.why: All stabilization policy (fiscal, monetary) targets the business cycle.
concepts.mnemonic: "PEAK–RECESSION–TROUGH–EXPANSION = PRT-E like 'Party Time Ends.'" Or: economy is a roller-coaster — peaks fall to troughs.
concepts.related: Unemployment, real GDP, recessions, expansions, NBER.

concepts.name: Unemployment Rate (calculation framing)
concepts.definition: Unemployment Rate = (Unemployed / Labor Force) × 100. Labor Force = Employed + Unemployed (people actively seeking work).
concepts.why: Excludes "discouraged workers" and those not seeking — hence a noisy real-world signal.
concepts.mnemonic: "ULF — Unemployed Looking Folks." Only people who LOOK count as unemployed. Couch + Netflix = not in labor force.
concepts.related: Labor force participation rate, frictional/structural/cyclical unemployment.

concepts.name: Inflation, Deflation, Price Stability
concepts.definition: Inflation = rising overall price level; deflation = falling overall price level; price stability = roughly constant.
concepts.why: A single good's price change is NOT inflation — inflation is about the AGGREGATE price level.
concepts.mnemonic: "Inflation = balloon Inflating (prices puffed up). Deflation = a flat tire." Hold a balloon when reviewing.
concepts.related: CPI, real vs. nominal, hyperinflation, debt deflation.

concepts.name: Economic Growth
concepts.definition: A sustained INCREASE in the maximum amount of goods/services an economy CAN produce (potential output). Shown as outward shift of PPC or LRAS.
concepts.why: Long-run growth dwarfs business cycle effects on living standards.
concepts.mnemonic: "Growth = the PPC GROWS outward." Distinguish from a recovery (movement TO the PPC, not OF it).
concepts.related: Productivity, real GDP per capita, technology, human capital.

concepts.name: Models & Ceteris Paribus
concepts.definition: A model is a simplified representation of reality. Ceteris paribus = "other things equal" assumption that isolates one variable.
concepts.why: Every economic claim ("if price rises, Qd falls") implicitly assumes ceteris paribus.
concepts.mnemonic: "Ceteris Paribus = Cetera (other things) Sleep." Hold everything else asleep while one variable wakes up.
concepts.related: Independent vs. dependent variables, comparative statics.

concepts.name: Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)
concepts.definition: Graph showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with current resources and technology, given full efficient use.
concepts.why: Showcases scarcity (boundary), opportunity cost (slope), efficiency (on vs. inside), and growth (outward shift).
concepts.mnemonic: "PPC = Possible-Produce-Cap." Inside = lazy economy; on = efficient; outside = dream.
concepts.related: Productive efficiency, allocative efficiency, opportunity cost.

concepts.name: Productive vs. Allocative Efficiency
concepts.definition: Productive efficiency = producing on the PPC (no waste). Allocative efficiency = producing the MIX of goods consumers most want (the right point ON the PPC).
concepts.why: Productive efficiency is necessary but NOT sufficient — an economy can be productively efficient but make all tanks and no bread.
concepts.mnemonic: "PRODUCTIVE = how MUCH; ALLOCATIVE = WHICH MUCH." Or: productive = no waste of inputs; allocative = no waste of preferences.
concepts.related: Pareto efficiency, marginal social benefit = marginal social cost.

concepts.name: Comparative Advantage
concepts.definition: An agent has comparative advantage in a good if their OPPORTUNITY COST of producing it is LOWER than another agent's.
concepts.why: It is THE explanation for why countries trade. Even an absolutely worse producer benefits from trading.
concepts.mnemonic: "COMPARATIVE = COMPARE costs (opportunity costs)." Picture Hank — terrible at everything, still wins at trade because he's comparatively less bad at coconuts.
concepts.related: Absolute advantage, terms of trade, specialization.

concepts.name: Absolute Advantage
concepts.definition: An agent has absolute advantage in producing a good if they can make MORE of it from a given quantity of resources (or use fewer resources per unit).
concepts.why: It is NOT the basis for trade. Mixing it up with comparative advantage is the most common AP error.
concepts.mnemonic: "ABSOLUTE = AMOUNT." Who produces a bigger absolute amount? Whoever does has absolute advantage.
concepts.related: Comparative advantage, productivity, specialization.

concepts.name: Terms of Trade
concepts.definition: The rate at which one good is exchanged for another. Mutually beneficial range: between the SELLER's opportunity cost (the floor) and the BUYER's opportunity cost (the ceiling).
concepts.why: Picks any terms outside this range and one party rejects trade.
concepts.mnemonic: "TERMS LIVE IN THE TUNNEL between the two opportunity costs." If outside the tunnel, no deal.
concepts.related: Comparative advantage, gains from trade.

concepts.name: Law of Demand
concepts.definition: All else equal, as price rises, quantity demanded falls (and vice versa). Demand curves slope downward.
concepts.why: Foundation for all microeconomic price theory; works through substitution and income effects.
concepts.mnemonic: "Higher price, Lower quantity = HP–LQ." Imagine a price tag pushing a customer downstairs.
concepts.related: Demand curve, substitution effect, income effect, Giffen goods (rare exception).

concepts.name: Demand Shifters (the TRIBE)
concepts.definition: Demand shifts when one of five things changes: Tastes, prices of Related goods (substitutes/complements), Income, number of Buyers, Expectations.
concepts.why: Every "what happens to demand" question reduces to: which TRIBE letter?
concepts.mnemonic: "TRIBE" — Tastes, Related goods, Income, Buyers, Expectations. (Krugman gives this mnemonic in the AP exam tip box.)
concepts.related: Movement along vs. shift, normal vs. inferior goods, substitutes vs. complements.

concepts.name: Substitutes vs. Complements
concepts.definition: Substitutes: rise in price of A → INCREASE in demand for B (e.g., coffee & tea). Complements: rise in price of A → DECREASE in demand for B (e.g., cars & gasoline).
concepts.why: Sign of cross-price elasticity. Substitutes give POSITIVE cross-price elasticity; complements NEGATIVE.
concepts.mnemonic: "SUBS = swap" (one replaces the other). "COMPLEMENTS = comrades" (they hang out together).
concepts.related: Cross-price elasticity.

concepts.name: Normal vs. Inferior Goods
concepts.definition: Normal: income ↑ → demand ↑. Inferior: income ↑ → demand ↓ (e.g., instant noodles, bus rides).
concepts.why: Determines sign of income elasticity. Inferior goods are the "downgrade" goods.
concepts.mnemonic: "INFERIOR = you DITCH it when you get RICHER." Casual dining replaces fast food when income rises.
concepts.related: Income elasticity, Engel curve, Giffen goods.

concepts.name: Movement Along vs. Shift of the Demand Curve
concepts.definition: A change in the good's own PRICE = movement along (change in quantity demanded). A change in any OTHER factor = shift (change in demand).
concepts.why: Mixing them up is the most common MCQ trap on the AP exam.
concepts.mnemonic: "PRICE moves ALONG; everything else SHIFTS." Or: "Own price stays on the curve; outside forces push the curve."
concepts.related: TRIBE shifters, supply-side analog.

concepts.name: Market Demand = Horizontal Sum
concepts.definition: Market demand at each price = sum of quantities demanded by all individuals at that price.
concepts.why: Tells you HOW to aggregate. Don't sum prices — sum quantities at the same price.
concepts.mnemonic: "HORIZONTAL = HEADS ACROSS." Line up everyone's Q at the same price and add across.
concepts.related: Aggregation, market supply (also horizontal sum).

concepts.name: Slope of a Curve
concepts.definition: Slope = Δy / Δx ("rise over run"). Linear curve: slope constant. Nonlinear curve: slope varies (use the arc method between two points for an average).
concepts.why: Slope of PPC = opportunity cost; slope of demand curve relates to elasticity; slope of TC curve = marginal cost.
concepts.mnemonic: "RISE OVER RUN, ECON IS WON." Sign of slope tells direction; magnitude tells sensitivity.
concepts.related: Elasticity, marginal cost, marginal product.

concepts.name: Law of Supply
concepts.definition: Other things equal, quantity supplied rises as price rises (positive slope).
concepts.why: Mirror image of law of demand; combined they generate equilibrium.
concepts.mnemonic: "Producers PUSH UP when prices PUSH UP" — both arrows point the same way.
concepts.related: Supply curve, quantity supplied, law of demand.

concepts.name: Five Shifters of Supply (I-RENT)
concepts.definition: Supply shifts when Input prices, prices of Related goods (substitutes/complements in production), Expectations, Number of producers, or Technology change.
concepts.why: Distinguishing shift vs. movement is THE most-tested AP/olympiad skill.
concepts.mnemonic: **I-RENT** — "I rent my factory: Inputs, Related goods, Expectations, Number of firms, Technology." A landlord (firm) rents capacity.
concepts.related: Movement along supply, change in supply, substitutes in production.

concepts.name: Substitutes vs. Complements IN PRODUCTION
concepts.definition: Two goods are substitutes in production if making more of one means making less of the other from the same inputs (gasoline/heating oil from crude). Complements in production are joint products (crude oil and natural gas from the same well).
concepts.why: Reverses sign convention students learn for consumption: rising price of a substitute in PRODUCTION decreases supply of the original good.
concepts.mnemonic: "Refinery vs. Oil Well." Refinery = rival outputs (substitute in production); Oil well = teammates (complement). Picture pumps that come up together.
concepts.related: Co-produced goods, supply shifters.

concepts.name: Equilibrium (Market-Clearing)
concepts.definition: Price at which Qd = Qs; no agent can do better by changing behavior.
concepts.why: Anchor of every comparative-statics question.
concepts.mnemonic: "Checkout line equilibrium": all lanes equal because shoppers rebalance until no lane is shorter.
concepts.related: Surplus, shortage, supply, demand.

concepts.name: Simultaneous Shift Rule
concepts.definition: When S and D shift in OPPOSITE directions, price is determinate, Q ambiguous. When in the SAME direction, Q is determinate, price ambiguous.
concepts.why: Single most common olympiad/AP trap.
concepts.mnemonic: **"SAME-Q, OPPOSITE-P"** — the variable that "wins" is whichever sees both forces pushing the same direction.
concepts.related: Comparative statics.

concepts.name: Price Ceiling Inefficiencies (4-pack)
concepts.definition: Effective ceilings cause (1) inefficiently low quantity, (2) inefficient allocation to consumers, (3) wasted resources from search, (4) inefficiently low quality. Plus black markets.
concepts.why: AP loves "list 3 inefficiencies of rent control."
concepts.mnemonic: **"LASQ-B"** — Low quantity, Allocation bad, Search wasted, Quality low, Black markets. Say it as "LASQ Bee."
concepts.related: Rent control, minimum wage (parallel), black market.

concepts.name: Price Floor Inefficiencies (4-pack mirror)
concepts.definition: Inefficiently low quantity, inefficient allocation of sales among SELLERS, wasted resources, inefficiently HIGH quality, plus illegal activity.
concepts.why: Mirror of ceiling; the trap is that floors also CUT quantity traded.
concepts.mnemonic: "FLOOR = HIGH quality, CEILING = LOW quality" — the inefficiency type matches the direction of the price distortion.
concepts.related: Minimum wage, agricultural price supports.

concepts.name: Quota Rent
concepts.definition: Wedge between demand price and supply price at the quota quantity; the rent earned by license-holders.
concepts.why: Explains why a NYC taxi medallion sold for $1M+.
concepts.mnemonic: Picture **Sunil's wrist sprain**: medallion owner rents $2/ride to driver Harriet — the $2 is "rent that lives in the gap between $6 (rider pays) and $4 (driver keeps)."
concepts.related: Deadweight loss, license, wedge.

concepts.name: Deadweight Loss (DWL)
concepts.definition: Value of mutually beneficial transactions prevented by a price/quantity intervention.
concepts.why: First introduction to welfare economics; reappears in tax incidence, monopoly, etc.
concepts.mnemonic: "Deadweight = Dead Trades" — a triangle of corpses (lost trades) between D and S to the right of the quota line.
concepts.related: Quota, surplus loss, efficiency.

concepts.name: Circular-Flow Identity
concepts.definition: Flow of money into any sector = flow out. Households' inflows (wages, interest, rent, profit, transfers) = outflows (taxes, consumption, private savings).
concepts.why: Justifies why income-, expenditure-, and value-added measures of GDP all match.
concepts.mnemonic: "What goes in MUST come out" — like a roundabout: every car that enters has to exit somewhere.
concepts.related: Disposable income, GDP, leakage/injection.

concepts.name: GDP — Three Equivalent Approaches
concepts.definition: Value-added (sum of each firm's sales − inputs), Expenditure (C + I + G + X − IM), Income (wages + interest + rent + profit). All equal.
concepts.why: Olympiad questions often disguise one method to test understanding of equivalence.
concepts.mnemonic: "VIE for GDP" — Value-added, Income, Expenditure all VIE to measure the same pie.
concepts.related: Aggregate spending, value added, factor income.

concepts.name: What's NOT in GDP (IF IF U)
concepts.definition: Excluded — Intermediate goods, Financial assets/transfer payments, Inputs used up, Foreign-produced goods, Used goods.
concepts.why: AP free-response gold mine ("does this count?").
concepts.mnemonic: **"IF IF U"** as the book prescribes — and add a story: "**IF IF U** sell stocks, **IF IF U** sell intermediate steel, **IF IF U** sell used cars — it doesn't count."
concepts.related: Final vs. intermediate, double-counting.

concepts.name: Real vs. Nominal GDP
concepts.definition: Nominal uses current prices; Real uses base-year prices (or chain-linking), stripping out inflation.
concepts.why: Comparing growth across years REQUIRES real GDP (the Venezuela example: 27% nominal but only 2% real growth).
concepts.mnemonic: "Real = Robbed of inflation" — real GDP has had inflation stolen from it, leaving only true growth.
concepts.related: GDP deflator, chain-linking, inflation rate.

concepts.name: Labor Force & Unemployment Definitions
concepts.definition: Labor force = Employed + Unemployed (actively looking ≤ 4 weeks). Population 16+ outside labor force does NOT count.
concepts.why: Discouraged workers, retirees, students, disabled are NOT unemployed. Underemployed (part-timers wanting full time) also not counted.
concepts.mnemonic: "AAA — Available, Actively looking, in past 4 weeks Ago." Need all three to count as unemployed.
concepts.related: U6, discouraged workers, marginally attached, underemployed, labor force participation rate.

concepts.name: Three Types of Unemployment (FSC)
concepts.definition: Frictional (search/transition), Structural (skill or wage-floor mismatch), Cyclical (recession-driven). Natural rate = Frictional + Structural.
concepts.why: Identification is heavily tested; cyclical = the only one that responds to monetary/fiscal policy.
concepts.mnemonic: **"FSC = Friction, Structure, Cycle"** — picture a car: Friction (worn brakes), Structure (broken chassis), Cycle (engine revs up & down). Natural = Friction + Structure (the car's built-in flaws).
concepts.related: Efficiency wages, minimum wage, unions, business cycle.

concepts.name: Real vs. Nominal Interest Rate
concepts.definition: Real rate = Nominal rate − Inflation rate (Fisher approximation).
concepts.why: Determines actual winners/losers from inflation. Unexpected inflation favors BORROWERS; unexpected disinflation/deflation favors LENDERS.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Borrowers Bless** Inflation, **Lenders Loathe** Inflation" (when it's unexpected). Picture a homeowner cheering while a bank cries.
concepts.related: Mortgage payments, gold standard, William Jennings Bryan.

concepts.name: Costs of Inflation (SMU)
concepts.definition: **Shoe-leather** (running to bank), **Menu** (relabeling), **Unit-of-account** (distorted contracts/taxes on phantom gains).
concepts.why: Classic AP free-response triple.
concepts.mnemonic: **"SMU"** — picture a Southern Methodist University student running to the bank (shoe-leather), changing the menu at a restaurant job (menu), and getting a confusing pay stub (unit-of-account).
concepts.related: Hyperinflation, German 1921–23, Brazil 1990s, Israeli 1980s.

concepts.name: Price Index Formula
concepts.definition: Price index in year t = (Cost of market basket in year t / Cost in base year) × 100. Base year index always = 100.
concepts.why: CPI, PPI, and GDP deflator all use this skeleton.
concepts.mnemonic: "Compare to BASE, multiply by 100, base year is HOME (100)." Base year is always home plate.
concepts.related: Inflation rate, CPI, market basket.

concepts.name: CPI Overstatement (3 reasons)
concepts.definition: CPI overstates true inflation due to (1) substitution bias (fixed basket misses consumer switching), (2) quality bias (improved products counted as price hikes), (3) innovation bias (new goods missed).
concepts.why: Indexing Social Security to CPI hands seniors a slight real-income raise each year.
concepts.mnemonic: "**SQI** — Substitution, Quality, Innovation — the three SQUIggly biases that bend CPI upward."
concepts.related: Boskin Commission (background), chain-weighting.

concepts.name: Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC)
concepts.definition: The fraction of an additional $1 of disposable income that a household spends on consumption; MPC = ΔC / ΔYD, with 0 < MPC < 1.
concepts.why: Determines the size of the spending multiplier = 1/(1−MPC). Higher MPC ⇒ bigger multiplier ⇒ bigger swings in real GDP from a given spending shock.
concepts.mnemonic: Picture MPC as a "leaky bucket." When $1 of income hits the bucket, MPC of it pours out as spending and MPS stays in (saved). The smaller the hole (low MPC), the less ripples through the economy. MPC + MPS = 1 (every dollar is either spent or saved).
concepts.related: MPS, spending multiplier, consumption function, autonomous consumption.

concepts.name: Spending Multiplier
concepts.definition: The ratio of the total change in real GDP to the autonomous change in aggregate spending that caused it; equals 1/(1−MPC) in a simple model with no taxes or imports.
concepts.why: Quantifies the chain reaction of how an initial spending change ripples through rounds of consumption to a much larger GDP change.
concepts.mnemonic: "Echo in a canyon." Shout $1 of new spending and the canyon echoes back 1 + MPC + MPC² + … . The echo dies out only because some sound (savings) gets absorbed each bounce. A canyon with hard rock walls (high MPC) echoes longer.
concepts.related: MPC, autonomous change in aggregate spending, tax multiplier, balanced-budget multiplier.

concepts.name: Autonomous Change in Aggregate Spending
concepts.definition: An initial rise or fall in aggregate spending at a given level of real GDP — the cause, not the result, of the multiplier chain reaction.
concepts.why: It's the "shove" that starts the multiplier; without distinguishing it from induced changes, you'll double-count.
concepts.mnemonic: "AUTO-nomous = self-driving." It moves on its own without GDP needing to change first. Like a car with no driver rolling downhill — the rolling causes the gravity push, not the other way around.
concepts.related: Spending multiplier, MPC, demand shock.

concepts.name: Consumption Function (aggregate form: C = A + MPC × YD)
concepts.definition: An equation/graph showing how aggregate consumer spending depends on aggregate current disposable income; A is autonomous consumption (intercept), MPC is the slope.
concepts.why: Translates the macro relationship between income and spending into a usable equation. Shifts from expected future income or wealth changes — NOT from current income (that's movement along the curve).
concepts.mnemonic: "Anchor + Anchor-chain." A is the boat's anchor that holds spending up even with zero income. MPC × YD is the chain — the more income flows out, the further the boat (consumption) drifts.
concepts.related: Permanent income hypothesis, life-cycle hypothesis, autonomous consumption.

concepts.name: Permanent Income Hypothesis (Friedman) & Life-Cycle Hypothesis
concepts.definition: Permanent income hypothesis: consumers base spending on expected long-term income, not just current income. Life-cycle hypothesis: consumers smooth consumption over their lifetime, saving in peak earning years and dissaving in retirement.
concepts.why: Explains why the consumption function shifts when expectations of future income or wealth change, even before current income changes.
concepts.mnemonic: "Marshmallow test for adults." Both hypotheses say people don't just gobble whatever marshmallows are in front of them now — they look ahead and smooth out the feast and famine years.
concepts.related: Consumption function shifts, aggregate wealth effects.

concepts.name: Planned vs. Unplanned (Inventory) Investment
concepts.definition: Planned investment = what firms intend to spend on capital, R&D, and structures. Unplanned inventory investment = the gap between expected and actual sales, ending up on the shelf (positive) or depleted (negative). Actual investment = Planned + Unplanned.
concepts.why: Rising unplanned inventories signal slowing demand (a leading recession indicator). Falling unplanned inventories signal a booming economy.
concepts.mnemonic: "Warehouse barometer." Inventories rising unexpectedly = an economic rain cloud coming (firms will cut output). Inventories vanishing fast = sunshine ahead (firms will ramp up).
concepts.related: Investment spending, business cycle, leading indicators.

concepts.name: Wealth Effect (of a change in the aggregate price level)
concepts.definition: A higher aggregate price level reduces the real purchasing power of consumers' financial assets (cash, bank accounts), making them feel poorer and cut consumption — and vice versa. One of two reasons AD slopes down.
concepts.why: Distinguishes the AD curve from a microeconomic demand curve — it's NOT about substituting away from a relatively pricier good.
concepts.mnemonic: "Wallet shrinkage." Imagine inflation shrinks the cash in your wallet like a sweater in a hot dryer — same number of bills, less buying power.
concepts.related: AD slope, interest rate effect, real vs. nominal values.

concepts.name: Interest Rate Effect (of a change in the aggregate price level)
concepts.definition: A higher aggregate price level forces people to hold more money for transactions, raising money demand and interest rates, which lowers investment and consumer spending. The second reason AD slopes down.
concepts.why: Provides the link between the price level and the loanable funds/money market that propagates into AD's slope.
concepts.mnemonic: "Crowded ATM." If prices double, everyone runs to the ATM to get more cash, jamming the lending market. The cost of borrowing (interest) shoots up, scaring off investors.
concepts.related: Wealth effect, money market, monetary policy.

concepts.name: Sticky Wages
concepts.definition: Nominal wages that are slow to fall during high unemployment and slow to rise during labor shortages, due to formal contracts and informal agreements.
concepts.why: This is the single reason SRAS is upward-sloping. When prices change but nominal wages don't (yet), profit per unit changes, and so does output.
concepts.mnemonic: "Wages set in Jell-O." Once wages are written into the contract, they're stuck in the jelly mold for a year or three — they wiggle only at renegotiation time.
concepts.related: SRAS slope, nominal wage, profit per unit, long-run flexibility.

concepts.name: Short-Run vs. Long-Run Aggregate Supply
concepts.definition: SRAS is upward-sloping because nominal wages are sticky. LRAS is vertical at potential output Y_P because all prices including wages eventually adjust.
concepts.why: Determines whether changes in AD have permanent effects on output (NO — only on prices in the long run) or only short-run effects (YES).
concepts.mnemonic: "Short shorts vs. tall jeans." SRAS is short and slanted (flexible in the short run); LRAS is a tall, vertical pole stuck in the ground at Y_P — try pushing it sideways and you just bend nothing.
concepts.related: Potential output, self-correcting economy, output gap.

concepts.name: Potential Output (Y_P)
concepts.definition: The level of real GDP the economy would produce if all prices, including nominal wages, were fully flexible — the horizontal intercept of LRAS.
concepts.why: It's the benchmark around which actual output fluctuates. Long-run growth = rightward shift of LRAS = growth in Y_P from more/better resources or tech progress.
concepts.mnemonic: "The economy's cruising altitude." Planes can dip below or climb above (turbulence = business cycle), but they always trend back to the optimal altitude set by engine quality (resources & tech).
concepts.related: LRAS, output gap, long-run growth.

concepts.name: Demand Shock vs. Supply Shock
concepts.definition: Demand shock = a shift of AD (P and Y move SAME direction). Supply shock = a shift of SRAS (P and Y move OPPOSITE directions). Stagflation = negative supply shock (P up, Y down).
concepts.why: Diagnosing which kind of shock hit the economy determines whether stabilization policy can help. Demand shocks are fixable with fiscal/monetary policy; supply shocks pose a brutal trade-off.
