concepts.mnemonic: "Same Same vs. Opposite Day." Demand shock = P and Y wear matching shirts (both up or both down). Supply shock = they wore mismatched shirts to school — one up, one down.
concepts.related: Stagflation, recessionary/inflationary gap, stabilization policy.

concepts.name: Recessionary Gap vs. Inflationary Gap
concepts.definition: Recessionary gap: actual GDP < potential output, so output gap is NEGATIVE, unemployment high, nominal wages will eventually fall. Inflationary gap: actual GDP > potential output, output gap POSITIVE, unemployment low, nominal wages will eventually rise.
concepts.why: Tells you the direction of self-correction (which way SRAS will eventually shift) and which type of fiscal policy is appropriate.
concepts.mnemonic: "Recession = Left, Right-side-up Inflation." On the AD-AS graph, draw SRAS∩AD to the LEFT of LRAS for a recessionary gap (under-shooting). To the RIGHT of LRAS for inflationary. Output gap formula: positive = inflationary, negative = recessionary.
concepts.related: Output gap, self-correcting economy, fiscal policy.

concepts.name: Self-Correcting Economy
concepts.definition: Over the long run, shocks to AD affect only the price level, not output, because nominal wages adjust and SRAS shifts to restore Y = Y_P.
concepts.why: It's the theoretical justification for laissez-faire ("In the long run we are all dead" — Keynes's retort) versus the case for active stabilization policy.
concepts.mnemonic: "Economic homeostasis." Like your body returning to 98.6°F after a fever (recessionary gap = cold sweats) or sunburn (inflationary gap = overheated). Slow but reliable.
concepts.related: Long-run equilibrium, Keynes, stabilization policy.

concepts.name: Stagflation
concepts.definition: Simultaneous stagnation (falling output, rising unemployment) and inflation (rising prices) — the signature of a negative supply shock.
concepts.why: Stabilization policy hits a brick wall: shifting AD right fights unemployment but worsens inflation; shifting AD left fights inflation but worsens unemployment.
concepts.mnemonic: "Stuck in tar AND on fire." Stagflation = the economy is stuck and burning at the same time. The 1970s OPEC oil shocks gave us the worst case.
concepts.related: Supply shock, OPEC, Phillips curve trade-off.

concepts.name: Fiscal Policy (Expansionary vs. Contractionary)
concepts.definition: Government use of spending (G), transfers, or taxes to shift AD. Expansionary = ↑G, ↓T, or ↑Transfers (shifts AD right). Contractionary = ↓G, ↑T, or ↓Transfers (shifts AD left).
concepts.why: Primary tool for closing recessionary or inflationary gaps in the short run. Subject to time lags (recognition, decision, implementation) that can backfire.
concepts.mnemonic: "Gas pedal (Ex-pand) vs. brake (Con-tract)." When the economy is sluggish, hit the gas: more G, fewer taxes, more transfers. When overheated, hit the brake: less G, more taxes, fewer transfers.
concepts.related: Stabilization policy, multipliers, automatic stabilizers, lags.

concepts.name: Tax Multiplier
concepts.definition: The factor by which a change in tax collections multiplies into a change in real GDP. Formula: −MPC / (1−MPC). It is negative (because tax increases reduce spending) and one less in absolute value than the spending multiplier.
concepts.why: A $1 of tax change has a smaller impact than $1 of government purchases because households save a portion (MPS) of any tax change.
concepts.mnemonic: "Taxes are weaker because they leak first." When G spends $1, all $1 hits AD. When the government cuts taxes by $1, only MPC × $1 actually gets spent — the rest is saved before it ever enters the economy.
concepts.related: Spending multiplier, balanced-budget multiplier, MPS.

concepts.name: Balanced-Budget Multiplier
concepts.definition: The factor by which an EQUAL increase in both G and T changes real GDP. Equals 1/(1−MPC) + [−MPC/(1−MPC)] = (1−MPC)/(1−MPC) = 1.
concepts.why: A balanced budget expansion is NOT neutral — it still increases GDP by the dollar amount of the spending change. Surprising and tested often.
concepts.mnemonic: "Tax-and-spend = exactly the spending." If government raises $50B in taxes and spends $50B, GDP rises by exactly $50B. The G effect overpowers the T effect by exactly $1 per $1 changed.
concepts.related: Spending multiplier, tax multiplier.

concepts.name: Automatic Stabilizers vs. Discretionary Fiscal Policy
concepts.definition: Automatic stabilizers = tax & transfer rules that automatically dampen the cycle (income taxes fall in recessions, UI rises). Discretionary fiscal policy = deliberate legislated changes in spending or taxes.
concepts.why: Automatic stabilizers reduce the size of multipliers and act with NO lag. Discretionary policy has long lags (recognition, decision, implementation).
concepts.mnemonic: "Cruise control vs. driver." Automatic = the car corrects speed without you touching anything (income tax, UI, food stamps). Discretionary = you grab the wheel and slam the brakes (a passed stimulus bill).
concepts.related: Time lags, MPC, marginal tax rate.

concepts.name: Savings–Investment Spending Identity
concepts.definition: S = I as an accounting identity. In an open economy: I = National Savings + Capital Inflow, where National Savings = Private Savings + Budget Balance.
concepts.why: Anchors macroeconomic flows. Budget deficits crowd out private investment unless offset by capital inflows from abroad.
concepts.mnemonic: "Pipe in = Pipe out." Whatever the economy saves (private + government + foreign) MUST equal what it invests — like water flowing through a closed system. No leaks.
concepts.related: Budget deficit/surplus, capital inflow, loanable funds.

concepts.name: Three Tasks of a Financial System
concepts.definition: A well-functioning financial system reduces (1) transaction costs, (2) financial risk (via diversification), and (3) illiquidity (via liquid asset markets).
concepts.why: Each financial asset type (loans, bonds, stocks, deposits, mutual funds) tackles one or more of these three. Match the asset to the problem.
concepts.mnemonic: "TRiL" — Transaction costs, Risk, Liquidity. Or: "A financial system makes trust cheap, fast, and flexible."
concepts.related: Financial intermediary, bonds, stocks, diversification.

concepts.name: Financial Asset Types (Loans, Bonds, Stocks, Bank Deposits, Loan-backed Securities)
concepts.definition: Loans = individual lending agreement, tailored but illiquid. Bonds = standardized IOUs, fixed interest, liquid. Stocks = ownership shares, higher risk & higher return than bonds, residual claim. Bank deposits = liquid claims on a bank. Loan-backed securities = pooled loans sold as shares (e.g., mortgage-backed).
concepts.why: Each is a different trade-off between return, risk, and liquidity. Bondholders get paid before stockholders in bankruptcy.
concepts.mnemonic: "Loans are LETTERS (custom), Bonds are BLANK CHECKS (standardized), Stocks are SHARES of the pie (ownership), Deposits are DEBIT-cards (liquid)."
concepts.related: Default risk, diversification, FDIC insurance.

concepts.name: Three Functions of Money
concepts.definition: Money is (1) a Medium of Exchange (paying for stuff), (2) a Store of Value (holding purchasing power over time), (3) a Unit of Account (the yardstick for prices). Mnemonic: M-S-U.
concepts.why: Solves the "double coincidence of wants" problem of barter. Failing as any one of the three (e.g., hyperinflation kills store-of-value) breaks the monetary system.
concepts.mnemonic: "Money MUST." M = Medium of exchange (USE it), U = Unit of account (MEASURE in it), S = Store of value (SAVE it). Music note: "MUST."
concepts.related: Commodity money, fiat money, hyperinflation.

concepts.name: M1 vs. M2
concepts.definition: M1 = currency in circulation + traveler's checks + checkable bank deposits (narrowest, most liquid). M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small CDs + money-market funds (near-moneys).
concepts.why: When the AP exam says "money supply," it usually means M1. Different policy tools affect different aggregates.
concepts.mnemonic: "M1 = M-ONE-thing-you-spend (cash and checking). M2 = M-TWO-thirds-you-can-spend-soon (add near-moneys)."
concepts.related: Money supply, near-moneys, liquidity, Federal Reserve.

concepts.name: Commodity Money, Commodity-Backed Money, and Fiat Money
concepts.definition: Commodity money has intrinsic value (gold, silver, cigarettes). Commodity-backed money is paper redeemable for a commodity. Fiat money has value only because the government declares it legal tender.
concepts.why: All modern major currencies are fiat. This allows flexible money supply but creates counterfeiting and inflation risk.
concepts.mnemonic: "Gold → IOU for Gold → Trust me, bro." Three stages of monetary evolution.
concepts.related: Money supply, Federal Reserve, inflation.

concepts.name: Present Value (PV) and Net Present Value (NPV)
concepts.definition: PV of $1 received in N years at interest rate r = $1 / (1+r)^N. NPV = sum of present values of benefits − sum of present values of costs. The right project rule: pick highest NPV.
concepts.why: Lets you compare cash flows arriving at different times on a common, "today" basis. Critical for capital budgeting, retirement planning, and lottery math.
concepts.mnemonic: "Discount escalator." Every year into the future, dollars ride one step DOWN the escalator (divide by 1+r). The further away, the smaller they become at the bottom (today).
concepts.related: Future value, interest rate, time value of money.

concepts.name: Bank Reserves and the Reserve Ratio
concepts.definition: Bank reserves = vault cash + bank's deposits at the Federal Reserve. Reserve ratio = reserves / deposits. Required reserve ratio = the minimum mandated by the Fed.
concepts.why: Determines how much of each deposit a bank can lend out, and thus the size of the money multiplier (1 / rr in the simplest model).
concepts.mnemonic: "Banker's seatbelt." Reserves are the safety belt that keeps the bank from crashing in a withdrawal panic. Required reserve ratio = minimum legal tightness.
concepts.related: Money multiplier, bank runs, FDIC.

concepts.name: Bank Run and Bank Regulation (Deposit Insurance, Capital Requirements, Reserve Requirements, Discount Window)
concepts.definition: Bank run = depositors rush to withdraw, fearing failure, which can self-fulfill. The U.S. defends against runs via (1) FDIC deposit insurance (up to $250k), (2) capital requirements (~7%), (3) reserve requirements, (4) Fed discount-window lending.
concepts.why: Without these protections, even a healthy bank can collapse from a panic. With them, modern bank runs are rare in developed economies.
concepts.mnemonic: "FDIC = Four Defenses In Crisis" — Insurance, Capital, Reserves, Discount window.
concepts.related: It's a Wonderful Life, IndyMac, FDIC, Federal Reserve.

concepts.name: Money Multiplier (Money Creation by Banks)
concepts.definition: When a bank holds fraction rr of deposits as reserves and lends out (1−rr), repeated rounds of deposit-and-lend create more money. In the simplest model, money multiplier = 1/rr.
concepts.why: Banks don't print money — they CREATE it through fractional-reserve lending. Each loan returns to the system as a deposit and gets re-lent.
concepts.mnemonic: "Bank multiplier = bouncing ball." A $1,000 deposit bounces 90% off the bank (loan), lands as another deposit, bounces 90% again, and so on, until the bounces die out. Total height of all bounces = $1,000/rr.
concepts.related: Reserve ratio, spending multiplier, fractional reserve banking.

concepts.name: Money Multiplier (1/rr)
concepts.definition: In a checkable-deposits-only system, the factor by which an initial increase in excess reserves multiplies into total deposits; more generally, the ratio of money supply to monetary base.
concepts.why: Students confuse the simple textbook multiplier (1/rr) with the real-world multiplier (~1.9 for M1) because people hold cash, which leaks out and doesn't support multiple deposits.
concepts.mnemonic: "rr in the basement: divide ONE by it to climb out of the bank vault into the whole money supply."
concepts.related: reserve ratio, excess reserves, monetary base, money supply.

concepts.name: Monetary Base vs. Money Supply
concepts.definition: Monetary base = currency in circulation + bank reserves. Money supply (M1) = currency in circulation + checkable deposits.
concepts.why: Reserves are in the BASE but NOT money supply; checkable deposits are in MONEY SUPPLY but NOT base. The only overlap is currency in circulation.
concepts.mnemonic: "Base has RESERVES (locked up); Supply has SPENDABLE deposits. Currency walks between both rooms."
concepts.related: Federal Reserve, fiat money, M1, M2.

concepts.name: Federal Funds Rate vs. Discount Rate
concepts.definition: Federal funds rate = interbank overnight lending rate (determined by supply/demand). Discount rate = rate the Fed itself charges banks at the discount window (set 1 pp above fed funds normally).
concepts.why: Trick exam Qs ask which the Fed "sets" directly. Fed targets fed funds rate (market-determined); Fed administratively sets the discount rate.
concepts.mnemonic: "Friends (Federal funds) lend friends; Discount comes from Daddy Fed."
concepts.related: open-market operations, reserve requirement, discount window.

concepts.name: Open-Market Operations
concepts.definition: Fed purchases or sales of U.S. Treasury bills with commercial banks to change the monetary base.
concepts.why: Buying T-bills INCREASES bank reserves & base; selling DECREASES them. This is the Fed's primary tool. The Fed never buys directly from the Treasury.
concepts.mnemonic: "BUY = bigger base. SELL = smaller supply." Or: "Open-market Buys Open the spigot."
concepts.related: monetary base, federal funds rate, Treasury bills.

concepts.name: Liquidity Preference Model (short-run interest rate)
concepts.definition: Interest rate is determined where money demand equals money supply in the money market.
concepts.why: Determines the SHORT-RUN interest rate; the loanable funds market follows. In the LONG RUN, the relationship reverses.
concepts.mnemonic: "LP = Liquidity Preferred in the Present (short run); LF = Loanable Funds for the Long-run Future."
concepts.related: money demand curve, money supply curve, nominal interest rate.

concepts.name: Crowding Out
concepts.definition: A government budget deficit raises the demand for loanable funds, pushing up the interest rate and reducing private investment spending.
concepts.why: Long-run cost of persistent deficits—reduces capital formation and long-run growth even apart from default risk.
concepts.mnemonic: "Big-G elbows little-i out of the loan line."
concepts.related: budget deficit, loanable funds, public debt.

concepts.name: Fisher Effect
concepts.definition: A 1-pp rise in expected inflation raises the equilibrium nominal interest rate by 1 pp, leaving the real interest rate unchanged.
concepts.why: Explains why high-inflation countries have high nominal rates without higher real rates—and why both S and D curves in loanable funds shift up together.
concepts.mnemonic: "Fisher fishes for the REAL rate—keeps it steady while NOMINAL swims up with inflation."
concepts.related: real vs. nominal interest rate, loanable funds, expected inflation.

concepts.name: Monetary Neutrality
concepts.definition: In the long run, changes in the money supply affect only the aggregate price level, not real GDP, real interest rates, or any other real variable.
concepts.why: Differentiates short-run (real effects) from long-run (purely nominal effects) policy outcomes—Fed cannot permanently boost output by printing money.
concepts.mnemonic: "Money is Neutered in the long run—it can only change PRICES, not REAL things."
concepts.related: long-run aggregate supply, classical model, quantity theory.

concepts.name: Cyclically Adjusted Budget Balance
concepts.definition: Estimate of what the budget balance would be if real GDP equaled potential output.
concepts.why: Strips out automatic stabilizer effects to reveal underlying fiscal stance—essential for sustainability analysis.
concepts.mnemonic: "Pretend the economy is HEALTHY—what would the deficit be?"
concepts.related: automatic stabilizers, potential output, structural deficit.

concepts.name: Implicit Liabilities
concepts.definition: Future spending promises (Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid) that act as debt but don't appear in standard debt statistics.
concepts.why: Makes the official debt/GDP figure understate true fiscal pressure—often the BIGGEST long-run concern.
concepts.mnemonic: "Three little pigs of implicit debt: Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid."
concepts.related: public debt, demographics, baby boomers, pay-as-you-go.

concepts.name: Inflation Tax & Seignorage
concepts.definition: Inflation tax = reduction in the real value of money held by the public when government prints money. Seignorage = revenue government earns from issuing currency.
concepts.why: Explains hyperinflation—governments that can't tax or borrow print money, eroding currency value.
concepts.mnemonic: "Seigneurs stamp coins; subjects pay the tax of shrinking wallets."
concepts.related: hyperinflation, fiat money, monetary base, Zimbabwe.

concepts.name: Demand-Pull vs. Cost-Push Inflation
concepts.definition: Demand-pull = AD shifts right ("too much money chasing too few goods"). Cost-push = SRAS shifts left (supply shock; e.g., oil prices).
concepts.why: Frequently tested directional question on AP/IEO. Note: cost-push also CAUSES output to fall (stagflation) while demand-pull raises output in short run.
concepts.mnemonic: "PULL the AD right; PUSH the SRAS left."
concepts.related: AD-AS model, supply shock, stagflation.

concepts.name: Phillips Curve (SR vs. LR) and NAIRU
concepts.definition: SRPC = negative trade-off between unemployment and inflation. LRPC = vertical line at NAIRU (Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment = natural rate).
concepts.why: Friedman/Phelps insight: trying to push U below NAIRU only accelerates inflation; trade-off vanishes in the long run.
concepts.mnemonic: "SHORT-run SLOPE, LONG-run LINE. NAIRU is the natural anchor."
concepts.related: expected inflation, natural rate, disinflation.

concepts.name: Liquidity Trap & Zero Bound
concepts.definition: Liquidity trap = situation where nominal interest rate is at zero and conventional monetary policy cannot stimulate further. Zero bound = nominal r cannot go negative because cash is a 0% option.
concepts.why: Explains why Fed/BoJ resorted to unconventional policies (QE) post-2008 and during Japan's Lost Decade.
concepts.mnemonic: "When r hits the FLOOR, monetary policy hits the WALL."
concepts.related: debt deflation, deflation, quantitative easing, Japan's Lost Decade.

concepts.name: Debt Deflation
concepts.definition: Falling price level increases the real burden of nominal debts, forcing borrowers to cut spending sharply; reduces aggregate demand and deepens slumps. Fisher (1933).
concepts.why: Key transmission channel that turned the 1929 crash into the Great Depression.
concepts.mnemonic: "Deflation makes Debts Demonically heavier."
concepts.related: Great Depression, liquidity trap, Irving Fisher.

concepts.name: Taylor Rule
concepts.definition: A rule for setting the federal funds rate: Federal funds rate = 1 + (1.5 × inflation rate) + (0.5 × output gap).
concepts.why: Approximates actual Fed behavior well; predicts direction of rate changes correctly.
concepts.mnemonic: "ONE plus ONE-and-a-HALF times inflation plus HALF times output gap—weight inflation more heavily."
concepts.related: inflation targeting, federal funds rate, output gap.

concepts.name: Keynesian Economics
concepts.definition: Macro framework attributing business cycles to shifts in AD (often from "animal spirits"); justifies active stabilization policy.
concepts.why: AP exams test the distinction from classical view: Keynes' SRAS slopes upward, so AD shifts move output.
concepts.mnemonic: "Keynes Keeps you Keeping busy" — government keeps spending in recessions.
concepts.related: Macroeconomic policy activism, animal spirits, AD shock.

concepts.name: Monetarism
concepts.definition: Doctrine (Milton Friedman) that GDP grows steadily if M grows steadily; central bank should follow a fixed-growth monetary rule.
concepts.why: Common test trap: students confuse monetarism with classical economics — but monetarism still accepts short-run real effects of M.
concepts.mnemonic: "Mr. Monetarist Marches the Money at a constant pace."
concepts.related: Quantity Theory of Money, monetary policy rule, velocity, Friedman, Schwartz.

concepts.name: Velocity of Money
concepts.definition: Ratio of nominal GDP to money supply (V = PY/M); the average number of times a dollar turns over per year.
concepts.why: If V is unstable, M-growth rule fails — this is why monetarism collapsed after 1980.
concepts.mnemonic: "V = Vivacious dollar — how often it parties."
concepts.related: Quantity Theory of Money, M1, MV=PY.

concepts.name: Natural Rate Hypothesis (Friedman–Phelps)
concepts.definition: To avoid accelerating inflation, the actual unemployment rate must equal the natural rate (NAIRU); any attempt to push U below NAIRU produces ever-rising inflation.
concepts.why: Implies LR Phillips curve is vertical; trade-off only short-run; widely accepted.
concepts.mnemonic: "NAIRU = No Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment — Natural Always Returns Up."
concepts.related: Long-run Phillips curve, expected inflation, stagflation.

concepts.name: Rational Expectations
concepts.definition: Households and firms optimally use *all* available information — including announced policy — when forming expectations.
concepts.why: Implies anticipated monetary policy is neutral even in the short run; predicts immediate (not gradual) build-in of expected inflation.
concepts.mnemonic: "Rational = Read the Fed press release."
concepts.related: New classical macroeconomics, Lucas critique, policy ineffectiveness.

concepts.name: Real Business Cycle Theory
concepts.definition: Business cycles caused by fluctuations in TFP / technology growth — i.e., SRAS shocks, not AD shocks.
concepts.why: Recovers the vertical-AS classical view; awarded 2004 Nobel (Kydland & Prescott).
concepts.mnemonic: "RBC = Recessions from Bad Computers" (tech slowdowns).
concepts.related: Total factor productivity, new classical macro, supply shocks.

concepts.name: New Keynesian Economics
concepts.definition: Argues market imperfections (menu costs, monopolistic price-setting) cause price stickiness, restoring Keynesian results despite rational expectations.
concepts.why: Reconciles rational expectations with real-world non-neutrality of money.
concepts.mnemonic: "Sticky prices, new Keynes."
concepts.related: Menu costs, monopolistic competition, price stickiness.

concepts.name: Political Business Cycle
concepts.definition: Unnecessary volatility caused by politicians juicing the economy before elections.
concepts.why: Justifies central-bank independence.
concepts.mnemonic: "Nixon 1972 — the GOAT of political business cycles" (per Rogoff).
concepts.related: Discretionary policy, central-bank independence.

concepts.name: Supply-Side Economics & Laffer Curve
concepts.definition: Belief that tax-rate cuts raise potential output enough that revenue may even rise; Laffer curve = revenue rises then falls as tax rates increase.
concepts.why: Trick: at *low* tax rates, a cut REDUCES revenue; only above the peak does a cut raise revenue.
concepts.mnemonic: "Laffer = Laughs at high tax rates" — bell-shaped curve.
concepts.related: Ronald Reagan, supply shocks, tax incentives.

concepts.name: Ricardian Equivalence
concepts.definition: Households see government spending today as future taxes; they reduce private spending to save for the tax bill, neutralizing fiscal stimulus.
concepts.why: Key anti-stimulus argument during the Great Recession.
concepts.mnemonic: "Ricardo Recognizes the Receipt — saves for tomorrow's tax."
concepts.related: Fiscal stimulus, debt, crowding out.

concepts.name: Rule of 70
concepts.definition: Years to double ≈ 70 / annual growth rate (in %).
concepts.why: Quick estimation tool, but only works for *positive*, steady growth rates.
concepts.mnemonic: "70 is heaven for doubling."
concepts.related: Real GDP per capita, long-run growth.

concepts.name: Labor Productivity
concepts.definition: Output per worker (or per hour); real GDP / number employed.
concepts.why: ~90% of LR per-capita GDP growth comes from productivity, not from putting more people to work.
concepts.mnemonic: "Productivity = Per-worker Power."
concepts.related: Physical capital, human capital, technology.

concepts.name: Physical Capital
concepts.definition: Manufactured goods (machines, buildings, infrastructure) used to produce other goods.
concepts.mnemonic: "Physical = you can Kick it."
concepts.related: Investment spending, depreciation, aggregate production function.

concepts.name: Human Capital
concepts.definition: Skill/education embodied in workers.
concepts.mnemonic: "Human = the head — Schooling adds to it."
concepts.related: Education, growth accounting.

concepts.name: Technology / TFP
concepts.definition: Technical means for producing goods; TFP = output achievable with given inputs.
concepts.mnemonic: "TFP shifts the curve UP." (movement along = capital; shift = tech.)
concepts.related: Growth accounting, real business cycle theory, productivity curve.

concepts.name: Diminishing Returns to Physical Capital
concepts.definition: Holding H and tech fixed, each extra unit of K/worker raises Y/worker by less than the previous unit.
concepts.why: Trick: only "other things equal" — if H or tech rises, returns may NOT diminish.
concepts.mnemonic: "Each tractor matters less than the first tractor."
concepts.related: Aggregate production function, growth accounting.

concepts.name: Convergence Hypothesis
concepts.definition: Poorer countries should grow faster than richer ones, narrowing income gaps.
concepts.why: Holds only conditionally — among wealthy/similar economies (Western Europe, Japan, U.S.) but NOT globally. "Conditional convergence" once you control for education, institutions, infrastructure.
concepts.mnemonic: "Catch-up only if you cleaned up your conditions."
concepts.related: East Asian miracle, Latin America, Africa.

concepts.name: Sustainable Growth
concepts.definition: Growth that can continue given limited natural resources and environmental impact.
concepts.why: Resource scarcity self-corrects via prices; environmental externalities don't — they require government intervention.
concepts.mnemonic: "Sustainable = Stays sustainable only with Smart policy."
concepts.related: Negative externality, carbon tax, cap and trade, Malthus.

concepts.name: Balance of Payments — Current Account
concepts.definition: Trade in goods + services + factor income + net transfers. Transactions that don't create future liabilities.
concepts.mnemonic: "Current = Cash on the spot for stuff/services/income."
concepts.related: Trade balance, financial account, BOP identity.

concepts.name: Balance of Payments — Financial Account
concepts.definition: Sales/purchases of assets between residents and foreigners; creates future liabilities.
concepts.mnemonic: "Financial = Future claims (assets)."
concepts.related: Current account, capital inflows.

concepts.name: Appreciation / Depreciation
concepts.definition: Appreciation = currency gains value vs. another; depreciation = loses value.
concepts.why: Common AP trap: when €/US$ rises, the dollar APPRECIATED and the euro depreciated.
concepts.mnemonic: "More foreign per buck = buck appreciated."
concepts.related: Real exchange rate, forex market.

concepts.name: Real Exchange Rate
concepts.definition: Nominal exchange rate × (Pdomestic / Pforeign) — adjusts for relative price-level differences.
concepts.why: Trade flows respond to *real*, not nominal, exchange rates. A nominal depreciation matched by domestic inflation leaves competitiveness unchanged.
concepts.mnemonic: "Real rate = real cheaper goods abroad."
concepts.related: Purchasing power parity, current account.

concepts.name: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)
concepts.definition: Nominal exchange rate that equates the cost of a common basket across countries.
concepts.why: Predicts LR exchange rates, not short-run. Big Mac Index is a fun proxy.
concepts.mnemonic: "Same Big Mac price = PPP."
concepts.related: Real exchange rate, Big Mac index.

concepts.name: Tariff vs. Import Quota
concepts.definition: Tariff = tax on imports (raises P, raises gov revenue). Quota = quantitative limit on imports (raises P, no gov revenue — rents go to license holders).
concepts.why: Students confuse "revenue" — only tariffs raise it for the government.
concepts.mnemonic: **T**ariff = **T**ax = **T**reasury gets paid. Quota = "Q for Quiet" — government collects no money.
concepts.related: protectionism, infant-industry argument, retaliation, NAFTA/TTIP.

concepts.name: Four-Step Macro Analysis (Module 45)
concepts.definition: (1) Starting point → (2) Pivotal event → (3) Initial (short-run) effects → (4) Secondary/long-run effects.
concepts.why: Free-response macro questions on the AP/IEO are scaffolded exactly this way.
concepts.mnemonic: "**S**tart, **P**ivot, **I**mpact, **L**ong-run" — **SPIL** the macro story.
concepts.related: AD-AS, money market, loanable funds, FX market, neutrality of money.

concepts.name: Substitution Effect vs. Income Effect
concepts.definition: Substitution effect = change in QD as a good becomes relatively cheaper/dearer (always opposes price change). Income effect = change in QD due to change in real purchasing power.
concepts.why: For most goods only substitution matters; income effect matters for big-budget goods. Goes opposite directions for inferior goods.
concepts.mnemonic: **S**ubstitution = **S**wapping; **I**ncome = **I** got poorer/richer.
concepts.related: Giffen goods, inferior goods, normal goods.

concepts.name: Giffen Good
concepts.definition: A good so strongly inferior that the income effect of a price rise *outweighs* the substitution effect, producing an upward-sloping demand curve.
concepts.why: Theoretical curiosity — the textbook says it has "never been validated" (Irish potatoes example).
concepts.mnemonic: "Giffen = Gives the law of demand a Geriatric, very rare exception."
concepts.related: inferior good, income effect dominance.

concepts.name: SPLAT — Determinants of PED
concepts.definition: Substitutes, Proportion of income, Luxury vs. necessity, Addictive/habit-forming, Time horizon.
concepts.why: AP frequently asks "which good has highest/lowest PED?"
concepts.mnemonic: **SPLAT** — splat your way to elasticity (more substitutes/luxury/time → more elastic; addictive/necessity → less elastic).
concepts.related: total-revenue test, long-run vs. short-run elasticity.

concepts.name: Total Revenue Test
concepts.definition: Inelastic D → P and TR move *together*; Elastic D → P and TR move *opposite*; Unit-elastic → TR unchanged.
concepts.why: Lets you classify elasticity without doing the arithmetic.
concepts.mnemonic: "**E**lastic = **E**nemies (price ↑, TR ↓); **I**nelastic = **I**nseparable (both move together)."
concepts.related: MR, monopoly pricing, demand curve segments.

concepts.name: Cross-Price Elasticity Sign Rule
concepts.definition: %ΔQa / %ΔPb. Positive → substitutes; Negative → complements; near zero → unrelated.
concepts.why: Sign matters — unlike PED, do NOT drop the minus.
concepts.mnemonic: "**P**ositive = **P**arallel goods (substitutes); **N**egative = **N**eed-each-other goods (complements)."
concepts.related: substitutes, complements, demand-shift factors.

concepts.name: Income Elasticity Sign Rule
concepts.definition: %ΔQd / %ΔIncome. Positive = normal good (>1 = income-elastic luxury; 0–1 = income-inelastic necessity). Negative = inferior good.
concepts.why: Engel curves & predicting which industries grow with GDP.
concepts.mnemonic: "**N**ormal = **N**umber positive; **I**nferior = **I**nverse (negative)."
concepts.related: Engel's law, luxury vs. necessity, agricultural-decline FYI.

concepts.name: Consumer Surplus (CS)
concepts.definition: Sum of (Willingness-to-pay − Price actually paid) over all buyers. Area below D, above P.
concepts.why: Welfare metric; used to evaluate price changes, taxes, trade policy.
concepts.mnemonic: "Buyers **B**ank a **B**onus" — CS is the bonus over the bare price.
concepts.related: willingness to pay, total surplus, market efficiency.

concepts.name: Producer Surplus (PS)
concepts.definition: Sum of (Price received − Seller's cost) over all sellers. Area above S, below P.
concepts.why: The producers' welfare gain from trade.
concepts.mnemonic: "Sellers **S**core **S**urplus" — above the supply, below the sale.
concepts.related: cost (opportunity cost), total surplus.

concepts.name: Total Surplus & Market Efficiency
concepts.definition: TS = CS + PS. Maximized at the competitive equilibrium quantity Qe; any other Q reduces TS.
concepts.why: Foundation of "markets are efficient" but caveat: equity, market failure, distribution.
concepts.mnemonic: "**M**arkets **M**aximize **M**utual gains" — three M's, three caveats (equity, failure, individual losers).
concepts.related: DWL, equity-efficiency tradeoff, gains from trade.

concepts.name: Tax Incidence Rule
concepts.definition: Tax burden falls more heavily on the side with *lower* elasticity. Inelastic side cannot escape.
concepts.why: Counter-intuitive: cigarette tax on producers ends up on consumers because PED of cigarettes is low.
concepts.mnemonic: "**I**nelastic = **I** pay; the **I**mmovable party gets stuck with the **I**nvoice."
concepts.related: PED, PES, statutory vs. economic incidence.

concepts.name: Deadweight Loss (DWL)
concepts.definition: Loss in total surplus from a tax/quota beyond what is transferred to government. Triangle pointing at efficient Q.
concepts.why: Measures pure inefficiency — value of mutually beneficial trades that don't happen.
concepts.mnemonic: "**D**WL = **D**isappearing **D**eals **W**asted."
concepts.related: tax revenue, lump-sum tax (no DWL), excise tax.

concepts.name: Lump-Sum Tax
concepts.definition: Fixed amount per person/entity regardless of behavior; does not distort quantity at the margin.
concepts.why: Efficient (no DWL) but typically inequitable. Thatcher's poll tax = real-world example.
concepts.mnemonic: "**L**ump = **L**eaves quantity un**L**altered."
concepts.related: progressive/regressive/proportional, efficiency-equity tradeoff.

concepts.name: Diminishing Marginal Utility
concepts.definition: Each additional unit of a good yields *less* additional utility than the prior unit (after some point).
concepts.why: Foundation of downward-sloping demand and the optimal-consumption rule.
concepts.mnemonic: "**3**rd slice of pizza is **3** times less thrilling than the 1st." Cassie's 9th clam = negative MU.
concepts.related: total utility, MU curve, satiation.

concepts.name: Optimal Consumption Rule
concepts.definition: Utility-maximizing bundle satisfies MUx/Px = MUy/Py = ... for all goods, subject to ΣPiQi = Income.
concepts.why: If MUx/Px > MUy/Py, reallocate dollar from y to x — net gain in utility.
concepts.mnemonic: "**E**qualize the **B**ang **P**er **B**uck" — EBPB.
concepts.related: budget constraint, marginal utility per dollar, indifference analysis.

concepts.name: Explicit vs. Implicit Cost; Accounting vs. Economic Profit
concepts.definition: Explicit = cash outlay; Implicit = forgone benefit (opportunity cost of own resources). Accounting profit = TR − explicit cost − depreciation. Economic profit = TR − explicit − implicit. Normal profit = zero economic profit.
concepts.why: A firm with positive accounting profit may have negative *economic* profit and should exit.
concepts.mnemonic: "**E**conomists **E**xclude nothing — they count what you **g**ave up."
concepts.related: opportunity cost, normal profit, depreciation.

concepts.name: Accounting Profit vs. Economic Profit
concepts.definition: Accounting profit = TR − explicit costs (and depreciation). Economic profit = TR − all opportunity costs (explicit + implicit).
concepts.why: Students forget the implicit cost of the owner's time and capital. A firm can have positive accounting profit but negative economic profit.
concepts.mnemonic: "Accountants Always Avoid implicit; Economists Examine Everything."
concepts.related: normal profit, implicit cost of capital, opportunity cost.

concepts.name: Normal Profit
concepts.definition: Economic profit = 0; firm earns just enough to cover all opportunity costs.
concepts.why: It is NOT zero accounting profit — students confuse "normal" with "nothing."
concepts.mnemonic: "Normal = Neutral; the firm is exactly indifferent between staying and leaving."
concepts.related: long-run PC equilibrium, break-even price.

concepts.name: Diminishing Returns to an Input
concepts.definition: Holding all other inputs fixed, each additional unit of the variable input adds less to output.
concepts.why: Confused with diseconomies of scale (which is a long-run concept where ALL inputs vary).
concepts.mnemonic: "DR is Short-run, RS is Long-run." DR = Diminishing Returns (one input fixed); RS = Returns to Scale (all inputs scale).
concepts.related: MPL curve, marginal cost rising, Malthus.

concepts.name: Spreading Effect vs. Diminishing Returns Effect
concepts.definition: Spreading = AFC falling because FC is divided over more units; Diminishing returns = AVC rising because each extra unit needs more variable input.
concepts.why: Together they produce U-shaped ATC: spreading dominates at low Q, diminishing returns dominates at high Q.
concepts.mnemonic: "SD curve: Spread Down at first, then Diminish Up."
concepts.related: U-shaped ATC, minimum-cost output.

concepts.name: Economies of Scale vs. Diminishing Returns
concepts.definition: Economies of scale = LRATC falls as Q rises (all inputs scale). Diminishing returns = MP of one variable input falls in short run.
concepts.why: Asked on AP routinely — diseconomies of scale is NOT the same as diminishing returns.
concepts.mnemonic: "Scale = Sizing the whole plant; Returns = Reaching for one more worker."
concepts.related: natural monopoly, increasing/decreasing returns to scale.

concepts.name: Sunk Cost
concepts.definition: A cost already paid and unrecoverable; irrelevant to forward-looking decisions.
concepts.why: Psychologically hard to ignore (loss aversion). Trick: future fixed cost is NOT sunk, but past spending is.
concepts.mnemonic: "Spilled milk — sob, don't subtract." Ignore.
concepts.related: short-run shut-down decision (FC behaves like a sunk cost in short run).

concepts.name: Price-Taker vs. Price-Maker
concepts.definition: A price-taker faces a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand at the market price; a price-maker faces the downward-sloping market demand.
concepts.why: Determines whether MR = P (PC) or MR < P (monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic comp.).
concepts.mnemonic: "Takers Take prices, Makers Move them."
concepts.related: perfect competition, demand curve shape.

concepts.name: Break-Even Price vs. Shut-Down Price
concepts.definition: Break-even price = minimum ATC (zero economic profit). Shut-down price = minimum AVC (firm produces only if P ≥ this).
concepts.why: Decision rule in short run differs from long run. AP loves the price-range trick.
concepts.mnemonic: "AVC = AVoid Closure; ATC = At Total Coverage." Below AVC → close.
concepts.related: short-run individual supply curve.

concepts.name: Quantity Effect & Price Effect (Monopoly MR)
concepts.definition: Quantity effect = +P from selling one more unit. Price effect = −ΔP × (prior units) because monopolist must lower price on all units.
concepts.why: Explains why MR < P for any price-maker (the marginal revenue curve lies BELOW the demand curve).
concepts.mnemonic: "Sell one More, Mark down all the Rest." More + Markdown = MR.
concepts.related: monopoly graph, oligopoly, monopolistic competition.

concepts.name: Allocative vs. Productive Efficiency
concepts.definition: Allocative efficiency = P = MC (producing the socially optimal mix). Productive efficiency = producing at minimum ATC (no resource waste).
concepts.why: PC achieves BOTH in long run; monopoly achieves NEITHER (P > MC, and Q is below min-ATC quantity if MR-MC crossing is at a smaller Q).
concepts.mnemonic: "Allocate at the Margin; Produce at the Minimum."
concepts.related: deadweight loss, long-run PC equilibrium.

concepts.name: Natural Monopoly
concepts.definition: A single firm has lower ATC than multiple firms over the relevant output range, due to large fixed costs and economies of scale.
concepts.why: Anti-trust action could RAISE costs; instead regulate to P = ATC.
concepts.mnemonic: "Naturally Needs Network — big pipes, one provider."
concepts.related: local utilities, average-cost pricing regulation.

concepts.name: Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI)
concepts.definition: Sum of squared market shares (in percent) of all firms in the industry. Range: ~0 (PC) to 10,000 (pure monopoly).
concepts.why: Squaring weights larger firms more heavily; AP may ask you to compute or interpret.
concepts.mnemonic: "HHI = Heavy on the Hefty Incumbents."
concepts.related: concentration ratio, oligopoly identification.

concepts.name: Single-Price Monopolist vs. Price Discrimination
concepts.definition: A single-price monopolist charges all consumers the same price; a price-discriminating monopolist charges different prices to different consumers for the SAME good.
concepts.why: Students confuse price discrimination with illegal practices; it's actually legal in most forms and INCREASES efficiency.
concepts.mnemonic: "Discriminate by Demand Elasticity" — charge inelastic buyers MORE.
concepts.related: perfect price discrimination, two-part tariff, volume discount, advance-purchase restriction.

concepts.name: Perfect Price Discrimination
concepts.definition: Each consumer pays exactly their willingness to pay; ALL consumer surplus becomes producer profit.
concepts.why: It is THE one monopoly case with zero deadweight loss — same Q as perfect competition!
concepts.mnemonic: "Perfect PD = Perfect Q (efficient), Perfect Zero CS (zero surplus to buyers)."
concepts.related: willingness to pay, allocative efficiency.

concepts.name: Conditions for Price Discrimination
concepts.definition: Firm must (1) have market power, (2) identify groups with different elasticities, (3) prevent resale.
concepts.mnemonic: "PER" — **P**ower, **E**lasticity differences, **R**esale prevention.

concepts.name: Oligopoly + Interdependence + Duopoly
concepts.definition: Few firms whose profits depend on each other's actions. A duopoly has two firms.
concepts.mnemonic: "Oligo = OH-NO they're watching me." Each firm watches what rivals do.
concepts.related: Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, 4-firm concentration ratio.

concepts.name: Collusion vs. Cartel
concepts.definition: Collusion = firms cooperate to raise joint profit. Cartel = formal collusive agreement.
concepts.why: Cartels are ILLEGAL in U.S. and EU; OPEC is legal only because it's a government cartel.
concepts.mnemonic: "Cartel = Contract"; "Collusion = Cooperation."

concepts.name: Quantity Effect vs. Price Effect
concepts.definition: Selling one more unit gives +P (quantity effect) but forces a price cut on all units (negative price effect).
concepts.why: The price effect is why MR < P for monopolists. Each oligopolist only feels the price effect on ITS OWN output, not its rivals' → individual incentive to cheat on collusive output.
concepts.mnemonic: "Q-up, P-down" — both effects always present for downward-sloping demand.

concepts.name: Prisoners' Dilemma
concepts.definition: A game where each player's dominant strategy makes both worse off than mutual cooperation.
concepts.mnemonic: "I Don't Trust You, You Don't Trust Me, We Both Lose." (IDTYYDTMWBL)
concepts.related: Nash equilibrium, dominant strategy, repeated games.

concepts.name: Dominant Strategy
concepts.definition: A player's best action regardless of what the opponent does.
concepts.mnemonic: "Dominant = always Done first." If circles cluster in one row (or column), it's the dominant strategy for that player.

concepts.name: Nash Equilibrium (Noncooperative Equilibrium)
concepts.definition: A strategy profile where no player wants to unilaterally change strategy.
concepts.mnemonic: "Nash = Nobody Adjusts, Solo-decision Holds."
concepts.related: A game may have 0, 1, or multiple Nash equilibria.

concepts.name: Tit-for-Tat
concepts.definition: Cooperate first, then mimic opponent's previous move. Rewards cooperation, punishes cheating.
concepts.why: Supports tacit collusion in REPEATED games even though individual cheating is the one-shot Nash equilibrium.
concepts.mnemonic: "Tit = Treat them as they Treat you."

concepts.name: Tacit Collusion
concepts.definition: Firms maintain high prices without formal agreement, often via repeated interaction or price leadership.
concepts.mnemonic: "Tacit = Together but silent."

concepts.name: Antitrust Policy
concepts.definition: Government efforts to prevent oligopolies from monopolizing or fixing prices. (Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890.)
concepts.mnemonic: "Anti-Trust = Anti-Cartel."

concepts.name: Price War, Price Leadership, Nonprice Competition
concepts.mnemonic: "When you can't COMPETE on price, COMPETE on EVERYTHING ELSE."

concepts.name: Monopolistic Competition
concepts.definition: Many firms, differentiated products, free entry/exit, no barriers, downward-sloping firm demand.
concepts.mnemonic: "Monop-Comp = Many Monopolists" — each is a tiny monopolist over its own niche.

concepts.name: Excess Capacity
concepts.definition: Monop. comp. firms in LR produce LESS than the quantity that minimizes ATC.
concepts.mnemonic: "Excess capacity = Empty seats" (e.g., food court vendors are never fully scaled up).

concepts.name: Product Differentiation (3 Types)
concepts.mnemonic: "SLQ — Style, Location, Quality" or "SeLeQt."

concepts.name: Derived Demand
concepts.definition: Demand for an input is derived from demand for the output it produces.
concepts.mnemonic: "Demand drips DOWN — output demand → input demand."

concepts.name: Marginal Revenue Product (MRP)
concepts.definition: Additional revenue from one more unit of an input = MPL × MR (or P, if PC product market).
concepts.why: A firm's MRP curve IS its factor demand curve.

concepts.name: Marginal Factor Cost (MFC)
concepts.definition: The additional cost of one more unit of an input. In PC labor markets, MFC = wage. In monopsony, MFC > wage (because hiring one more raises wages for ALL workers).
concepts.mnemonic: "Monopsony's MFC is Mighty More than the wage."

concepts.name: Economic Rent
concepts.definition: Payment to a factor in excess of the minimum needed to employ it.
concepts.mnemonic: "Rent = Reward beyond Required."
concepts.related: Producer surplus is the goods-market analog. Land tax has no DWL because supply is fixed.

concepts.name: Backward-Bending Labor Supply
concepts.definition: At low wages, substitution effect dominates → more labor supplied. At high wages, income effect dominates → less labor supplied.
concepts.mnemonic: "Bend at the Bonus" — when wages get really high, you'd rather take vacation.

concepts.name: Monopsony
concepts.definition: A single buyer of an input. Pays a wage BELOW competitive wage and hires LESS labor than competitive equilibrium.
concepts.mnemonic: "Mono-PSO-ny = One-Pays-Squat-Only."

concepts.name: Cost-Minimization Rule
concepts.definition: Adjust inputs until MP per dollar is equal across all factors: MPL/W = MPK/r.
concepts.mnemonic: "Bang per buck must be balanced."

concepts.name: Marginal Productivity Theory of Income Distribution
concepts.definition: In competitive factor markets, each factor is paid the equilibrium MRP of the last unit hired.
concepts.why: Explains WHY labor gets ~70% — labor's equilibrium MRP × quantity = ~70% of total income.

concepts.name: Compensating Differentials
concepts.definition: Wage premiums (or discounts) for unpleasant/dangerous (or pleasant) jobs of equivalent skill.
concepts.mnemonic: "Compensate for Crap" — dirtier/more-dangerous job → higher pay.

concepts.name: Efficiency Wages
concepts.definition: Above-equilibrium wages paid to motivate workers and reduce turnover.
concepts.why: Creates a wage floor → labor surplus → some unemployment.
concepts.mnemonic: "Efficiency wages = Extra to Encourage Effort."

concepts.name: Compensating Differentials
concepts.definition: Wage premium paid for unpleasant, dangerous, or undesirable job attributes.
concepts.why: Reconciles wage disparity with marginal-productivity theory — risky jobs (test pilots, oil-rig workers) pay more even with identical skill.
concepts.mnemonic: "**C**ompensating = **C**ash for **C**risk." If your job could kill you, the market pays you extra for sticking around.
concepts.related: Efficiency wages, human capital, MRP.

concepts.name: Efficiency-Wage Model
concepts.definition: Firms voluntarily pay ABOVE-equilibrium wages to elicit higher productivity, lower turnover, and reduce shirking.
concepts.why: Creates persistent wage rigidity and unemployment surplus; explains wage gaps unrelated to skill differences.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Efficient = Expensive** — pay more so they care more." Like overpaying a babysitter so they won't quit or scroll TikTok while watching the kid.
concepts.related: Surplus of labor, market failure in labor markets.

concepts.name: Marginal Social Cost of Pollution (MSC)
concepts.definition: The additional cost society bears from one more unit of pollution.
concepts.why: Upward-sloping because environment can absorb a little but harm rises faster as pollution accumulates.
concepts.mnemonic: "MSC climbs — the **M**ore **S**moke, the more **C**asualties."
concepts.related: MSB, socially optimal pollution, Pigouvian tax.

concepts.name: Marginal Social Benefit of Pollution (MSB)
concepts.definition: Additional benefit to society from emitting one more unit — i.e., the cost the polluter SAVES by not having to abate.
concepts.why: Counterintuitive but crucial — abatement is costly, so allowing some pollution saves real resources.
concepts.mnemonic: "MSB falls because **clean air gets pricier the cleaner it already is**" (low-hanging fruit picked first).
concepts.related: Avoidance cost, MSC, Q_OPT.

concepts.name: Coase Theorem
concepts.definition: If property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low enough, private bargaining will reach the efficient outcome regardless of who initially holds the rights.
concepts.why: Suggests externalities don't always need government — but real-world transaction costs (many parties, legal fees, holdouts) usually prevent Coase from working at scale.
concepts.mnemonic: "**C**oase = **C**heap deals **C**ure externalities." If two people can negotiate over coffee, no regulator needed.
concepts.related: Internalizing externalities, transaction costs, property rights.

concepts.name: Pigouvian Tax/Subsidy
concepts.definition: Tax (subsidy) set equal to the marginal external cost (benefit) at the socially optimal quantity.
concepts.why: Forces decision-makers to internalize the externality; achieves Q_OPT at minimum total cost.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Pig**ouvian = **Price**-tag the externality." Pin a dollar sign on the side effect.
concepts.related: Emissions tax, tradable permits, MEC, MEB.

concepts.name: Tradable Emissions Permits / Cap-and-Trade
concepts.definition: Government caps total pollution and issues permits that polluters can buy/sell; market price emerges.
concepts.why: Cost-effective like a tax (MB of pollution equalized across polluters) AND lets regulators fix quantity precisely.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Cap** the total, **trade** the toxin." Permits flow to firms where abatement is most expensive.
concepts.related: Pigouvian tax, EU ETS, U.S. SO₂ acid-rain program.

concepts.name: Environmental Standards
concepts.definition: Rules specifying limits or required actions for producers/consumers.
concepts.why: Inflexible — forces uniform cuts even when costs differ → fails to equalize marginal benefit of pollution → inefficient.
concepts.mnemonic: "**S**tandards are **S**tiff — no flex, no trade." Like making every kid do the SAME number of push-ups regardless of fitness.
concepts.related: Clean Air Act, emissions tax, cap-and-trade.

concepts.name: Network Externality
concepts.definition: Value of a good rises with the number of OTHER users (fax-machine effect).
concepts.why: Generates "winner-take-all" markets (operating systems, social networks); congestion is a NEGATIVE network externality.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Net**works = **More** users = **More** value."
concepts.related: Technology spillover, switching costs.

concepts.name: Excludability vs. Rivalry (4-Type Matrix)
concepts.definition: Excludable = can prevent non-payers; Rival = one person's use prevents another's. Combinations → private, public, common-resource, artificially-scarce.
concepts.why: Determines whether markets can efficiently supply the good.
concepts.mnemonic: "**ER** = **E**xclude/**R**ival → 4 quadrants: - **PR**ivate (E + R) like a **PR**ivate **PR**operty; - **PUB**lic (¬E + ¬R) like a **PUB**lic park sewer; - **CR**owded (¬E + R) like ocean fish = **C**ommon **R**esource; - **AS** (E + ¬R) = **A**rtificially **S**carce like cable TV."
concepts.related: Free-rider, overuse, technology spillover.

concepts.name: Free-Rider Problem
concepts.definition: Nonexcludability makes rational consumers refuse to pay, hoping others will → undersupply of the good.
concepts.why: Core market failure for public goods; justifies government provision via taxation.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Free** ride = **F**ailure to **fund**." Group project shirker = mini free rider.
concepts.related: Public goods, common resources, voting paradox.

concepts.name: Vertical Summation of Demand for Public Goods
concepts.definition: Because public goods are nonrival, the social MB of one unit = SUM of every consumer's individual MPB at that quantity.
concepts.why: Differs sharply from PRIVATE-good demand (horizontal sum). Determines correct efficient quantity for public goods.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Public = Pile up** (vertical); **Private = line up** (horizontal)."
concepts.related: MSB = ΣMPB, MSC = MSB, efficient quantity.

concepts.name: Overuse / Tragedy of the Commons
concepts.definition: Common-resource users ignore the depletion cost imposed on others → MSC > MPC → market quantity exceeds efficient quantity.
concepts.why: Why fisheries collapse, why highways congest, why aquifers deplete.
concepts.mnemonic: "**No owner → no caretaker**." If everyone owns the cake, everyone takes a slice and the cake vanishes.
concepts.related: Pigouvian tax, ITQs (individual transferable quotas), property rights.

concepts.name: Artificially Scarce Good
concepts.definition: Excludable but nonrival; producer charges P > 0 even though marginal cost of additional consumption is zero → under-consumption.
concepts.why: Pricing above zero creates DWL, but charging zero leaves no incentive to produce.
concepts.mnemonic: "**A**rtificially **S**carce = **A**ccess **S**hut for **profit**." Pay-per-view movies, software licenses.
concepts.related: Patents/copyright, monopoly pricing.

concepts.name: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890)
concepts.definition: First major U.S. antitrust law; outlaws restraints of trade AND monopolization (acts that create/maintain monopoly).
concepts.why: Being a monopoly isn't illegal — MONOPOLIZING (taking acts to create monopoly) is.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Sh**erman **Sh**uts down **Sh**enanigans" but doesn't punish lucky monopolists.
concepts.related: Clayton 1914, FTC 1914, Microsoft case.

concepts.name: Clayton Antitrust Act (1914)
concepts.definition: Clarifies Sherman by outlawing specific behaviors: price discrimination, exclusive dealing, tying, anticompetitive mergers, and interlocking directorates.
concepts.why: Made antitrust enforcement operational; merger reviews still use Clayton standards (HHI, concentration ratios).
concepts.mnemonic: "**Clay-PEAT-IDol**: **P**rice discrim, **E**xclusive dealing, **A**cquisitions/mergers, **T**ying, **I**nter**l**ocking **d**irectorates."
concepts.related: Sherman, FTC, HHI.

concepts.name: Federal Trade Commission Act (1914)
concepts.definition: Created the FTC; outlaws unfair competition, price fixing, output restrictions, barriers to entry.
concepts.why: Provides an enforcement agency beyond the DOJ.
concepts.mnemonic: "**FTC = Fair Trade Cop**."
concepts.related: Sherman, Clayton, antitrust.

concepts.name: Marginal-Cost Pricing vs. Average-Cost Pricing (Natural Monopoly)
concepts.definition: MC pricing sets P = MC (allocatively efficient but loss for natural monopoly because MC < ATC); AC pricing sets P = ATC (zero economic profit, undersupply).
concepts.why: Captures the regulator's trade-off between efficiency and the need to avoid subsidies.
concepts.mnemonic: "**MC = Most Customers** (but money-losing); **AC = Acceptable Compromise**."
concepts.related: Natural monopoly, economies of scale, deadweight loss.

concepts.name: Poverty Threshold vs. Poverty Rate
concepts.definition: Threshold = the income line below which a family is officially "poor" (adjusted for cost of living, NOT for standard of living). Rate = % of population below threshold.
concepts.why: Because threshold isn't updated to rising standards, an economy can grow richer without lowering poverty.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Threshold** = **the line**, **Rate** = **the share**."
concepts.related: Means-tested programs, working poor.

concepts.name: Mean vs. Median Household Income
concepts.definition: Mean = total income / number of households. Median = middle income.
concepts.why: Mean is skewed by extreme outliers (a billionaire walks into the room); median tracks the typical household.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Mean** = **Manipulated** by millionaires; **Median** = **Middle of the room**."
concepts.related: Lorenz curve, Gini.

concepts.name: Lorenz Curve & Gini Coefficient
concepts.definition: Lorenz curve plots cumulative % of income vs. cumulative % of population. Gini = A / (A+B); 0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality.
concepts.why: Standard cross-country inequality comparison. U.S. ~0.477; Sweden ~0.25; Brazil ~0.6.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Gini grows as the Lorenz line bows.**"
concepts.related: Income quintiles, redistribution.

concepts.name: Means-Tested vs. Non-Means-Tested Programs
concepts.definition: Means-tested = benefits only for those below an income/wealth cutoff (TANF, SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, EITC). Non-means-tested = available regardless of income (Social Security, Medicare, Unemployment Insurance).
concepts.why: Means-testing controls cost but creates "notch" problems (high effective marginal tax rates that discourage work).
concepts.mnemonic: "**Means** = **Money-line gate**; **Non-means** = **Open to all**."
concepts.related: Notch problem, in-kind benefits, negative income tax.

concepts.name: Negative Income Tax (EITC)
concepts.definition: Government supplements low-wage workers' earnings; effectively a wage subsidy for the poor.
concepts.why: Preserves work incentives unlike traditional welfare; only workers with earnings qualify.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Earn more, owe negative tax**."
concepts.related: EITC, working poor, notch problem.

concepts.name: Notch Problem
concepts.definition: Earning $1 more can cost a recipient $X in benefits, creating high effective marginal tax rates and reducing work incentives.
concepts.why: Means-testing's hidden cost; modern programs use sliding-scale phase-outs.
concepts.mnemonic: "**Notch** = **No use working harder**."
concepts.related: EITC phase-out, sliding-scale benefits.

concepts.name: Private (Asymmetric) Information
concepts.definition: Information that some market participants have and others do not (e.g., used-car seller knows car is a lemon; buyer doesn't).
concepts.why: Distorts decisions and kills mutually beneficial trades; leads to either adverse selection or moral hazard.
concepts.mnemonic: "PRIVATE = Person Really Is Veiling Asymmetric Truth Entirely."
concepts.related: adverse selection, moral hazard, signaling, screening.

concepts.name: Adverse Selection ("lemons problem")
concepts.definition: Hidden information about TYPE/QUALITY before the transaction — sellers self-select the worst items to sell (Akerlof, 1970).
concepts.why: Causes the "adverse-selection death spiral" in insurance — healthy people drop out, premiums rise, more drop out, market collapses.
concepts.mnemonic: "Adverse selection = picked BEFORE the deal" (Type problem). Lemons sour the whole batch.
concepts.related: moral hazard, screening, signaling, lemons, health insurance.

concepts.name: Moral Hazard
concepts.definition: Hidden ACTIONS after the transaction — insured party behaves more recklessly because someone else bears the cost.
concepts.why: Justifies deductibles, co-pays, franchise restaurants, sales commissions, and "skin in the game."
concepts.mnemonic: "Moral hazard = misbehavior AFTER the deal." (Action problem.)
concepts.related: deductible, principal-agent, "bail out" expectations, financial crisis.

concepts.name: Screening vs. Signaling vs. Reputation
concepts.definition: Three tools to defeat asymmetric info. Screening = uninformed party uses observable proxies (e.g., GPA, ZIP code for auto insurance). Signaling = informed party takes a costly action only worth taking if they're high-quality (warranty, college diploma). Reputation = long-run track record substitutes for one-time costly signal.
concepts.mnemonic: "Screen FROM outside, Signal FROM inside, Reputation OVER time."
concepts.related: adverse selection, warranties, education as signal.

concepts.name: Indifference Curve
concepts.definition: Locus of consumption bundles yielding the same total utility for a given consumer.
concepts.why: Lets us derive consumer optima without needing to quantify utils (ordinal, not cardinal).
concepts.mnemonic: "I-C = Identical Contentment."
concepts.related: indifference curve map, MRS, ordinary goods, tangency condition.

concepts.name: Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS)
concepts.definition: The rate at which a consumer is willing to give up good Y for one more unit of good X while keeping utility constant. MRS = MU_X / MU_Y = −(slope of indifference curve).
concepts.why: At the optimum, MRS = price ratio P_X/P_Y. Diminishing MRS gives indifference curves their convex shape.
concepts.mnemonic: "MRS = More-for-Reduction Swap."
concepts.related: diminishing marginal utility, tangency condition, relative price rule.

concepts.name: Tangency Condition / Relative Price Rule
concepts.definition: Optimal bundle occurs where the budget line is tangent to the highest reachable indifference curve, i.e., MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
concepts.why: Equivalent to the optimal consumption rule (MU_X/P_X = MU_Y/P_Y). Income changes shift BL parallel; price changes rotate it.
concepts.mnemonic: "TANGENT = The Angle Now Genuinely Equals Net Trade-ratio." Slopes match → no cheaper rearrangement exists.

concepts.name: Simple vs. Compound Interest
concepts.definition: Simple interest accrues only on principal. Compound interest accrues on principal PLUS previously earned interest.
concepts.why: Over long horizons, compounding dominates — $100 at 5% for 3 years: $115 simple vs. $115.76 compound annually vs. $115.97 semiannually.
concepts.mnemonic: "Simple is straight, Compound is on top of compound."
concepts.related: APR, APY, Rule of 72, time value of money.

concepts.name: Rule of 72
concepts.definition: Years to double an investment ≈ 72 / (annual % return). Or, required rate ≈ 72 / years to double.
concepts.why: Lightning-fast mental check on growth questions — e.g., 1% rate → 72 years; 6% → 12 years; 9% → 8 years.
concepts.mnemonic: "72: Two-Seven-Two = the Twin doubler."
concepts.related: Rule of 70 (used in macro growth chapter — slightly more precise for continuous compounding).

concepts.name: APR vs. APY
concepts.definition: APR = annual percentage rate (nominal, ignores compounding within the year). APY = annual percentage yield (effective, includes compounding).
concepts.why: APY > APR whenever compounding occurs more often than once a year. Always compare savings accounts on APY, loans on APR.
concepts.mnemonic: "Y for Yours-actually-earned, R for Raw-rate."

concepts.name: Marginal/Progressive Tax vs. Effective Tax Rate
concepts.definition: A marginal tax rate applies to the LAST dollar earned (the bracket you're in); the effective (average) rate = total tax / total income. Progressive system: marginal rate rises with income.
concepts.why: Most-tested trick: students confuse "I'm in the 25% bracket" with "I pay 25% on all my income." You don't — only on the slice ABOVE the bracket threshold.
concepts.mnemonic: "Brackets are STAIRS, not floors."
concepts.related: proportional tax, regressive tax, FICA, payroll withholding.

concepts.name: Stocks vs. Bonds vs. Mutual Funds vs. ETFs
concepts.definition: Stocks = ownership shares (residual claim). Bonds = debt (fixed-income claim). Mutual funds = professionally managed bundle, priced once per day. ETFs = bundle of securities that trades intraday like a stock.
concepts.why: Risk/return ranking: stocks > mutual stock funds > bond funds > bonds > savings/CDs. Higher expected return demands higher risk.
concepts.mnemonic: "SBMF = Stocks Boss, Bonds Borrow, Mutuals Mingle, ETFs Exchange Mingled."

concepts.name: IRA / Roth IRA / 401(k) / 403(b)
concepts.definition: Tax-advantaged retirement accounts. Traditional IRA & 401(k) = pre-tax contributions, deferred tax on withdrawal. Roth IRA = after-tax contributions, tax-free growth and withdrawal. 401(k) = employer-sponsored; 403(b) = same but for schools/non-profits.
concepts.why: Roth vs. Traditional choice depends on whether you expect a higher tax rate now or in retirement. Employer matching = "free money" — never leave it on the table.
concepts.mnemonic: "Roth pays Right-now, Traditional pays Tomorrow."

concepts.name: Defined Benefit vs. Defined Contribution Plans
concepts.definition: Defined benefit (pension) = employer guarantees a fixed monthly payout in retirement; employer bears investment risk. Defined contribution (401(k)/403(b)) = contribution is fixed, payout depends on market returns; employee bears risk.
concepts.why: DC plans are now the norm because they shift risk off employers. Explains decline of pensions.
concepts.mnemonic: "Benefit = Boss's risk; Contribution = Citizen's risk."

concepts.name: Net Worth
concepts.definition: Net worth = Assets − Liabilities. Tracks wealth (a STOCK), not income (a FLOW).
concepts.why: A high earner with high debt may have lower net worth than a modest earner who saves consistently. "Income makes you look rich; net worth makes you rich."
concepts.mnemonic: "Worth = What you Own − What you Owe."

concepts.name: Credit Score (FICO weights)
concepts.definition: FICO range 300–850, weights: Payment history 35% / Credit utilization 30% / Length of history 15% / Type-of-credit mix 10% / New-credit applications 10%.
concepts.why: 65% of your score is just "pay on time + don't max out cards." Closing your oldest card hurts (shortens history + raises utilization).
concepts.mnemonic: "PUNTA: Pay (35) Use (30) Number-of-years (15) Type (10) Applications (10)."

concepts.name: Deductible (in Insurance)
concepts.definition: Out-of-pocket amount the insured must pay before the insurer pays anything.
concepts.why: Reduces moral hazard (you still have skin in the game) AND screens for type (low-risk types choose high deductibles for lower premiums).
concepts.mnemonic: "Deductible = Discipline-fee."

concepts.name: 8 Major Types of Insurance
concepts.definition: Health, Disability, Life (term vs. permanent), Auto (collision/comprehensive/liability/PIP/uninsured-motorist), Homeowner's, Renter's, Long-term Care (LTC), Umbrella.
concepts.mnemonic: "HD-LAH-RLU" or "Healthy Doctors Live At Home, Rent Little Umbrellas."

concepts.name: Diversification
concepts.definition: Investing in multiple assets with unrelated/independent risks to reduce overall portfolio risk.
concepts.why: Idiosyncratic risk can be diversified away; systematic (market) risk cannot.
concepts.mnemonic: "Don't carry all your eggs in one wallet."

concepts.name: Upside-Down Loan
concepts.definition: When the outstanding loan balance exceeds the market value of the collateral (e.g., car loan balance > car's current value).
concepts.why: Selling or trading requires paying out of pocket. Mortgage version = "underwater" mortgage; central to the 2008 housing crisis.
concepts.mnemonic: "Upside-down = your wallet's been flipped."

formulas.name: Opportunity Cost (from a PPC)
formulas.equation: Opportunity cost of one unit of X = (Δ units of Y given up) / (Δ units of X gained)
formulas.variables: X is the good you're producing more of; Y is the good given up.
formulas.units: Expressed as "units of Y per unit of X." Always positive when stated as a cost. The slope of the PPC equals the NEGATIVE of the opportunity cost of the x-axis good.
formulas.example: If Tom's PPC goes from (28 fish, 9 coconuts) to (40 fish, 0 coconuts), opportunity cost of one fish = 9 / 12 = 3/4 coconut.

formulas.name: Slope of a Linear Curve
formulas.variables: Δy = change in vertical-axis variable; Δx = change in horizontal-axis variable.
formulas.units: Same sign as the rise-to-run ratio. Negative if curve slopes downward.

formulas.name: Area of a Right Triangle (under/above a linear curve)
formulas.variables: base = horizontal leg; height = vertical leg.
formulas.units: Always positive; units = (units of x) × (units of y) / 2 (e.g., dollars when price × quantity).
formulas.example: Triangle with base 4 and height 6 has area = (1/2)(4)(6) = 12. This is the formula you'll reuse for consumer surplus, producer surplus, and deadweight loss.

formulas.name: Labor Force / Unemployment Rate
formulas.equation: Labor Force = Employed + Unemployed.  Unemployment Rate = (Unemployed / Labor Force) × 100.
formulas.variables: Employed (currently working for pay); Unemployed (actively seeking but not working).
formulas.units: Both expressed in numbers of people; rate in %. Discouraged workers, retirees, full-time students are NOT in the labor force.
formulas.example: If a country has 120M employed and 8M unemployed: Labor force = 128M; U-rate = 8 / 128 = 6.25%.

formulas.name: Mutually Beneficial Terms-of-Trade Range
formulas.equation: Price_seller's OC < Trade price < Price_buyer's OC (for one unit of the good).
formulas.variables: Each side's opportunity cost of producing the good in question.
formulas.units: Expressed in units of the OTHER good per unit of THIS good.
formulas.example: Hank's OC of one coconut = 1/2 fish. Tom's OC of one coconut = 4/3 fish. Mutually beneficial price for coconuts: any rate strictly between 1/2 fish and 4/3 fish per coconut. At 1 fish/coconut, both gain.

formulas.name: Inflation Rate (year-over-year)
formulas.variables: P_year1, P_year2 = price index (or price level) in the two consecutive years.
formulas.units: Reported in percent. Positive = inflation; negative = deflation; declining but positive = disinflation (NOT deflation).

formulas.name: Price Index
formulas.equation: `Price index_year_t = (Cost of market basket_t / Cost of market basket_base) × 100`
formulas.variables: Cost of basket = Σ (Q_base × P_t) using fixed base-year quantities.
formulas.units: Dimensionless; base year index = 100 by construction.
formulas.example: Basket of 200 oranges + 50 grapefruit + 100 lemons costs $95 pre-frost, $175 post-frost. Index post-frost = (175/95) × 100 = 184.2.

formulas.name: GDP Expenditure Approach
formulas.variables: C = consumer spending, I = investment spending (incl. inventory change), G = government purchases of goods+services (NOT transfers), X = exports, IM = imports.
formulas.units: Nominal $ unless deflated. Net exports (X − IM) can be negative.

formulas.name: Value Added (per firm)
formulas.equation: `Value added = Value of sales − Cost of intermediate inputs purchased`
formulas.variables: Sales = top-line revenue; intermediate inputs = goods bought from other firms and used up in production.
formulas.units: Summed across all firms → GDP, avoiding double counting.
formulas.example: Auto firm sells car for $21,500, bought $9,000 of steel. Value added = $12,500. Add to steel firm's $4,800 and ore firm's $4,200 → $21,500 GDP.

formulas.name: Unemployment Rate
formulas.variables: Labor force = Employed + Unemployed. Unemployed = jobless AND actively searching in past 4 weeks AND available.
formulas.units: Percent. Denominator excludes those not in labor force (retirees, students, discouraged workers).
formulas.example: Population 16+ = 12M, Employed = 5M, Unemployed = 1M. LF = 6M. UE rate = 1/6 × 100 = 16.67%.

formulas.name: Labor Force Participation Rate
formulas.variables: LF = Employed + Unemployed; Population 16+ is the eligible pool.
formulas.units: Percent.
formulas.example: LF = 6M, Pop 16+ = 12M → LFPR = 50%.

formulas.name: Real Interest Rate (Fisher approximation)
formulas.variables: r = real interest rate, i = nominal interest rate, π = inflation rate.
formulas.units: Can be negative if inflation exceeds nominal rate.
formulas.example: Loan at i = 5%; unexpected inflation π = 5%. Real rate r = 0%. Borrower effectively got an interest-free loan; lender lost in real terms.

formulas.name: GDP Deflator
formulas.variables: Nominal GDP at current prices; Real GDP at base-year prices.
formulas.units: = 100 in base year by construction. Captures economy-wide prices (broader than CPI's consumer basket).
formulas.example: If nominal GDP doubles ($10T → $20T) but real GDP unchanged at $10T, deflator goes from 100 → 200 → economy-wide prices doubled.

formulas.name: Real GDP (base-year prices)
formulas.variables: Q_i,t = quantity of good i in year t; P_i,base = price of good i in base year.
formulas.units: Strips out price changes, isolates output change.

formulas.name: Quota Rent
formulas.variables: P_demand(Q) = the price consumers will pay for Q units (height of D at Q); P_supply(Q) = price producers need to receive (height of S at Q).
formulas.units: $/unit. Equals market price of a tradable license. Zero if quota set above equilibrium.
formulas.example: Swordfish quota of 7M lb. At Q=7M, P_d = $18, P_s = $12. Quota rent = $6/lb; a license is worth $6 per pound of catch authorized.

formulas.name: Marginal Propensity to Consume
formulas.variables: ΔC = change in consumer spending; ΔYD = change in disposable income.
formulas.units: Dimensionless; always between 0 and 1. MPS = 1 − MPC.
formulas.example: If disposable income rises by $10,000 and spending rises by $7,500, MPC = 7,500/10,000 = 0.75 (so MPS = 0.25).

formulas.name: Spending Multiplier
formulas.variables: MPC = marginal propensity to consume; MPS = marginal propensity to save.
formulas.units: Dimensionless and always ≥ 1 (since 0 < MPC < 1).
formulas.example: MPC = 0.8 → multiplier = 1/(1−0.8) = 1/0.2 = 5. So a $60 million increase in G raises real GDP by 5 × $60 million = $300 million.

formulas.name: Tax Multiplier
formulas.variables: MPC = marginal propensity to consume.
formulas.units: Always NEGATIVE (tax increase reduces spending). Absolute value is exactly 1 less than the spending multiplier.
formulas.example: MPC = 0.75 → tax multiplier = −0.75/0.25 = −3. A $20 billion tax CUT increases real GDP by −3 × (−$20B) = +$60 billion.

formulas.name: Balanced-Budget Multiplier
formulas.variables: Applies when ΔG = ΔT (equal change in spending and taxes).
formulas.units: Always equals 1, regardless of MPC.
formulas.example: Government raises both G and T by $100 billion. Real GDP increases by exactly $100 billion (regardless of whether MPC is 0.5 or 0.9).

formulas.name: Output Gap
formulas.equation: `Output gap = [(Actual real GDP − Potential GDP) / Potential GDP] × 100`
formulas.variables: Actual = current real GDP; Potential = Y_P (full-employment GDP).
formulas.units: Expressed as percent. Positive = inflationary gap; Negative = recessionary gap; Zero = long-run equilibrium.
formulas.example: Potential output = $1,000B, actual = $1,200B → output gap = (200/1000) × 100 = +20% (inflationary gap).

formulas.name: National Income Accounting Identity (AD components)
formulas.variables: C = consumer spending; I = investment spending; G = government purchases; X = exports; IM = imports.
formulas.units: All in same units (e.g., 2005 dollars for real GDP). Net exports (X − IM) can be negative.

formulas.name: Actual Investment Spending
formulas.variables: I_Planned = intended investment; I_Unplanned = unplanned inventory investment (can be negative).
formulas.units: Dollars; unplanned can be negative when sales exceed expectations.
formulas.example: A firm plans to invest $500M but sells 100,000 fewer cars than expected at $20,000 each ($2B unsold inventory). Actual I = $500M + $2B = $2.5B (with $2B classified as unplanned inventory buildup).

formulas.name: Aggregate Consumption Function
formulas.variables: C = aggregate consumer spending; A = aggregate autonomous consumption; MPC = marginal propensity to consume; YD = aggregate disposable income.
formulas.units: All dollar values; A and MPC are exogenous in the short run.
formulas.example: A = $1.6 trillion, MPC = 0.5, YD = $2.0 trillion → C = 1.6 + 0.5(2.0) = $2.6 trillion.

formulas.name: Profit Per Unit (basis of SRAS slope)
formulas.equation: `Profit per unit = Price per unit − Production cost per unit`
formulas.variables: Both per unit of output.
formulas.units: Dollars per unit; positive = produce more; negative = produce less.
formulas.example: Aggregate price level rises 10% but nominal wages (sticky) only rise 2%; profit per unit rises and producers expand output → upward-sloping SRAS.

formulas.name: Present Value of $1 in N Years
formulas.variables: r = annual interest rate (decimal); N = number of years.
formulas.units: Dollars; r must be in decimal (5% = 0.05).

formulas.name: Future Value of $1 in N Years
formulas.variables: r = interest rate (decimal); N = years.
formulas.units: Dollars; assumes compound interest.

formulas.name: Net Present Value (NPV)
formulas.variables: t = time of each cash flow; r = discount rate.
formulas.units: Dollars; positive NPV = profitable; pick highest among alternatives.
formulas.example: Project: pay $10 today, receive $115 in one year, r = 10%. NPV = −10 + 115/1.10 = −10 + 104.55 = $94.55.

formulas.name: Reserve Ratio
formulas.variables: Reserves = vault cash + deposits at the Fed; Deposits = total bank deposits.
formulas.units: Decimal or percent; required reserve ratio is the legal minimum.
formulas.example: Bank has $100,000 in reserves and $1,000,000 in deposits → rr = 0.10 = 10%.

formulas.name: Money Multiplier (Simple Model)
formulas.equation: `Money multiplier = 1 / rr` (assuming no cash leakage, banks hold no excess reserves)
formulas.variables: rr = required reserve ratio.
formulas.units: Dimensionless; total deposits created from initial reserve injection = (initial deposit) × (1/rr).
formulas.example: rr = 10% → money multiplier = 10. A new $1,000 deposit can support up to $10,000 in total checkable deposits across the banking system.

formulas.name: Money Multiplier (simple)
formulas.variables: rr = required reserve ratio (as a decimal).
formulas.units: rr must be expressed as a decimal (10% = 0.10). The multiplier is dimensionless. Only applies in a checkable-deposits-only system with no excess reserves and no cash leakage.
